en: Mahāyānasaṃgraha, Fascicle One.
Composed by Bodhisattva Asaṅga;
translated by Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha.
Chapter One: On the Superior Characteristics of the Basis; Chapter One: On Various Names. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* is the teaching of the Abhidharma as well as the Mahāyāna Sūtras.

Before the Buddha, the World-Honored One, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Skillfully Entering the Meaning of the Mahāyāna Phrases, desiring to reveal that the Mahāyāna possesses superior merits, spoke these words based on the Mahāyāna teachings:
"The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten superior characteristics; what they have taught is peerless and surpasses other teachings."

The ten superior characteristics are: first, the superior characteristic of the basis for what is to be known; second, the superior characteristic of what is to be known; third, the superior characteristic of the entry into what is to be known; fourth, the superior characteristic of the cause and fruit of entry; fifth, the superior characteristic of the distinctions in the cultivation of the cause and fruit of entry; sixth, the superior characteristic of the training in ethical discipline based on those distinctions in cultivation; seventh, the superior characteristic of the training in mental concentration based therein; eighth, the superior characteristic of the training in wisdom based therein; ninth, the superior characteristic of the tranquility that is the fruit of training; and tenth, the superior characteristic of the differentiation of knowledge.
By virtue of these ten superior characteristics, that which is taught by the Tathāgata surpasses other teachings.
Explaining the words and phrases of the sūtras in this manner reveals that the Mahāyāna is truly the word of the Buddha.
Furthermore, how does this brief explanation demonstrate that the Mahāyāna is superior to other teachings?
This brief explanation now reveals that these ten meanings exist only in the Mahāyāna and are absent from the Hīnayāna.
What are these ten? They are as follows:

the ālayavijñāna is designated as the characteristic of the basis for that which is to be known; and the three natures (trisvabhāva): [the imagined nature, the dependent nature, and the perfected nature].

The first is the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva), the second is the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva), and the third is the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva); these are called the characteristics of that which is to be known.
The teaching of Consciousness-Only (vijñaptimātra) is called the characteristic of the entry into that which is to be known.
The six pāramitās are called the characteristics of entering into cause and fruit.
The ten stages (bhūmi) of a bodhisattva are called the characteristics of the distinctions in the cultivation of cause and fruit.
The precepts received, maintained, and guarded by a bodhisattva are called the characteristics of the training in ethical discipline (*śīla-śikṣā*) within the distinctions of cultivation.
The *śūraṃgama* and *ākāśagarbha* samādhis are called the characteristics of the training in mind (*citta-śikṣā*).
Non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) is called the characteristic of the training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*).
Non-abiding nirvāṇa (*apratisthita-nirvāṇa*) is called the characteristic of the quiescence that is the fruit of the training (*śikṣā-phala-śānti-lakṣaṇa*).

The three bodies of the Buddha—the *svābhāvika-kāya*, the *sāmbhogika-kāya*, and the *nirmāṇa-kāya*—these three are said to be the characteristics of the fruit of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).

These ten points exist only within the Mahāyāna and differ from the Hīnayāna; therefore, they are called "supreme," for the Blessed Buddha taught these ten meanings solely for the sake of bodhisattvas.
According to the Mahāyāna, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten superior characteristics; that which they teach is peerless and surpasses other teachings.
Furthermore, how do these ten superior characteristics of the peerless teaching manifest the Mahāyāna?

This is the Tathāgata’s correct teaching, which excludes the Hīnayāna as definitively not being the Mahāyāna; for among the teachings of the Hīnayāna, one has never seen even a single one of these ten meanings explained, whereas they are seen explained only within the Mahāyāna.

Furthermore, these ten meanings are able to draw forth unsurpassed bodhi; they are accomplished in accordance with one another without contradiction, so that all sentient beings may attain the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
And he spoke in verse:
One should know the basis and its characteristics, The entry, the cause and fruit, and the distinctions in cultivation,
The three trainings, the fruit, cessation, Wisdom, and what is subsumed within the Unsurpassed Vehicle.
These ten meanings do not exist elsewhere; seeing them as the cause of enlightenment, the Buddha taught the Mahāyāna, for it is superior by virtue of explaining these ten meanings.
Why are these ten meanings explained in this specific order?

When a bodhisattva first begins their training, they should first contemplate all phenomena according to their actual causes and conditions; through this contemplation, they should develop wisdom regarding the twelve links of dependent origination.

Subsequently, they should discern the essential nature and characteristics of dependently originated phenomena, whereby, through wisdom, they may abandon the dual faults of superimposition and denial.

In this way, through correct cultivation, one should thoroughly penetrate the true characteristics of the objects of focus as they truly are; subsequently, one should be liberated from all hindrances.

Once the mind has thoroughly penetrated the true characteristics of what is to be known, the six perfections previously practiced should be further perfected and purified so that they are no longer subject to regression, by virtue of the internal purity of the mental faculty.
Next, regarding the perfections subsumed under internal purity, one should cultivate any one of them according to the distinctions of the ten stages over three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
Subsequently, the three trainings of a bodhisattva should be brought to fulfillment.
Once these are perfected, the fruit of this training—nirvāṇa and unsurpassed enlightenment—should subsequently be attained.
Such is the sequence for cultivating the ten topics.
Within this sequential exposition, the entirety of the Mahāyāna is brought to fulfillment.
This should be understood as the initial explanation.
Based on this, it is established by name as the *ālayavijñāna*.
In what place did the Blessed One speak of this consciousness, and by what name did he designate it as the *ālayavijñāna*?
As the Blessed One said in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-mūla-kārikā*:
"This realm is without beginning; It is the support for all phenomena.
If there are various paths, they exist; And there is the attainment of nirvāṇa."
In the Abhidharma, a verse further states:
"All phenomena abide supported by the store; it is the consciousness of all seeds, therefore it is named Ālaya;
I have taught this for the sake of the superior persons."
These two verses from the Āgama testify to the substance and the name of this consciousness.
Why does the Buddha say that this consciousness is named *ālaya*?
Because all impure phenomena (*aśubha-dharma*) that have arisen are hidden within it as effects, and because this consciousness is hidden among all phenomena as their cause.
Furthermore, because all sentient beings store this consciousness within themselves and grasp at it as a self, it is called the *ālayavijñāna*.
As stated in the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*, a verse from the *Anupūrvasamudgata-parivarta* says:
"The appropriating consciousness is profound and subtle; The seeds of phenomena flow forth constantly."
Regarding that which I do not declare to be the self, ordinary people grasp at as a self.
Why is this consciousness also called the *ādāna-vijñāna* (appropriating consciousness)?
Because it is able to appropriate all material sense-faculties and serves as the basis for the appropriation of all rebirths.
Why is this? Because the material sense-faculties are grasped and maintained by this consciousness, remaining unimpaired and undestroyed until the end of the continuum.

Furthermore, at the time of actualizing rebirth, because it is capable of producing the appropriated aggregates (*upādāna-skandha*), the bodies of the six realms of existence are all thus appropriated.
Because it grasps and maintains the objects of appropriation through consciousness, it is called *ādāna*.
Alternatively, it is called "mind" (*citta*), as the Blessed One said:
"Mind, mentation, and consciousness."
The mind (manas) is of two kinds:
first, because it serves as the immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for the arising of that [consciousness], the consciousness that has just ceased is the mind;
second, because it serves as the basis for the arising of consciousness, it is also the mind.
Second, there is the afflicted manas, which is constantly associated with four afflictions:
first, the view of a self-identity; second, the conceit "I am"; third, self-love; and fourth, ignorance. This consciousness is the basis for the other afflicted consciousnesses.
This afflicted consciousness arises from one basis, is defiled by a second, and is able to discern objects and their succession;
these two are called *manas*.
How is it known that there is a defiled mind?

If this mind did not exist, then solitary ignorance (*avidyā*) could not be said to exist; furthermore, this dharma would be non-existent, as it is similar to the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*).
Why is this? Because these five consciousnesses would simultaneously have their own respective supports, namely the sense organs such as the eye;
furthermore, the designation "mind" (manas) would then be devoid of meaning.
Furthermore, the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) should not differ. Why?
Because the attainment of non-conception is characterized by the presence of defiled mental states (*kliṣṭa-citta*), whereas the attainment of cessation is not so.
If it were not so, these two meditative attainments would necessarily be indistinguishable.

Furthermore, throughout the duration of a single lifetime in the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*), it would follow that this state is untainted (*anāsrava*) and free from fault, because it would be devoid of defilement—provided that within it there were no view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) nor the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*).

Furthermore, the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) arises at all times throughout virtuous, non-virtuous, and neutral states of mind. If it were not so, then because the grasping at a self would only be associated with non-virtuous minds, the notions of "I" and "mine" could only function within those [non-virtuous] states, and would not function within virtuous or neutral states.
If one posits that two minds arise simultaneously, this fault does not occur;
however, if one posits [ignorance] as functioning in association with the sixth consciousness, this fault arises.
There is no独行 (independently wandering) ignorance, nor is there anything similar to it in the five sensory consciousnesses.
The two meditative attainments are without distinction; the term "mind" (manas) would then lack its referent.

In the state of non-conception, there is no grasping at a self; throughout the duration of a single lifetime, within the wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral states, the grasping at a self ought not to arise.
Without a defiled mind, there is no [self-grasping]; since the two and the three are contradictory, and because these do not exist anywhere, the grasping for a self cannot arise.
By realizing the true meaning, or by obstructing it so that it does not arise, [the self-grasping is abandoned].
Constantly operating in all states, it is called "solitary ignorance.
Because this mind is defiled, it is categorized as indeterminate (avyākṛta) and is always associated with the four afflictions.

For example, the afflictions of the form and formless realms are obscured-neutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), because the defilements of these two realms are concealed by *śamatha*; thus, this mind constantly arises without ceasing its discursive investigation (*vitarka*).
The third substance cannot be found apart from the ālayavijñāna; therefore, the ālayavijñāna is established as the manas, and depending upon this as its seed, the other consciousnesses arise.
Why is this *manas* further called "mind" (*citta*)?
Because it is a collection of various seeds of habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*).
Why is the characteristic of this mind not taught in the Śrāvaka vehicle, yet the names *ālayavijñāna* and *ādānavijñāna* are taught there?
Because it is subsumed within a subtle sphere of experience.

Why is this? Śrāvakas do not possess the superior station for attaining the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*); therefore, this teaching is excluded for them. Since they fulfill their original vows through the attainment of [their own] wisdom, it is not taught to them.
All bodhisattvas should possess a superior station in order to attain the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna); therefore, the Buddha has taught this. Why is this?
Because it is impossible to attain unsurpassed enlightenment if one is devoid of this wisdom.
Furthermore, this consciousness has been revealed by the Tathāgata under different names within the Śrāvaka vehicle.
As stated in the *Ekottarika Āgama*:

"Because the world delights in the *ālaya*, loves the *ālaya*, is habituated to the *ālaya*, and clings to the *ālaya*, the Tathāgata teaches the True Dharma for the sake of extinguishing the *ālaya*. Because the world desires to hear it with joy, they lend an ear, apply attention, and desire to know; they arouse right effort and thereby attain the extinction of the *ālaya*, even unto practicing the Tathāgata’s True Dharma and its semblance."
With the appearance of the Tathāgata in the world, this first rare and inconceivable dharma manifests in the world.

Just as with the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), this *Tathāgatotpattisambhavanirdeśa-caturvidhaguṇasūtra* has already manifested that consciousness within the Śrāvaka vehicle through a different perspective.

Furthermore, in the Āgamas of the Mahāsāṃghika school, this consciousness is manifested through its specific designation as the "root-consciousness" (mūlavijñāna), just as a tree depends upon its roots.
The Mahīśāsaka school also describes this consciousness by another name, calling it the "aggregate that persists until the end of saṃsāra" (āsaṃsārikaskandha).
Why is this? Because although at times the continuity of form and mind may appear to be severed, within this mind those seeds are never interrupted.
One should know that these depend upon the ādāna, the ālaya, the citta, the mūlavijñāna, and the bhavāṅga-skandha.
By virtue of this name, the ālayavijñāna has already become the established path of authority within the Hīnayāna.
Furthermore, there are other masters who maintain that these three—citta, manas, and vijñāna—are merely different names for the same meaning.
This interpretation is not correct; since the meanings of *manas* and *vijñāna* have already been seen to differ, one should know that the meaning of *citta* must likewise differ.

Furthermore, there are other masters who maintain that when the Tathāgata spoke of the world’s delight in the *ālaya* as previously described, he was referring to the five aggregates of grasping (*pañcopādānaskandha*) therein as being called *ālaya*.
Furthermore, there are other masters who maintain that pleasant sensation associated with desire is called the ālaya.
Still others maintain that the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is called the ālaya.
These various masters are deluded regarding the ālayavijñāna; based on both scripture (āgama) and meditative attainment, they have thus formed such attachments.
Because they follow the teachings and practices of the Hīnayāna, the doctrines established by these masters do not accord with reason.
If there is someone who is not deluded regarding the ālayavijñāna and establishes this consciousness by means of the terminology of the Hīnayāna, its meaning is most excellent.
Why is it most excellent?

If one were to grasp the appropriated aggregates (upādānaskandha) as the ālaya, then when one is born in those states of existence within any of the miserable destinies where there is exclusively the sensation of suffering, [the ālaya would be impossible].

This aggregate of clinging is most loathsome and contrary; within this aggregate of clinging, there is nothing whatsoever that is truly desirable, and it is unreasonable for sentient beings to find joy in it. Why is this so?
The sentient beings therein constantly aspire for the cessation of the appropriated aggregates so that they do not arise again.
If this pleasant sensation were associated with desire, such a sensation would be absent from the fourth dhyāna up through the higher realms.

If a person has already attained this feeling, they will develop a sense of revulsion toward it when seeking the higher realms; therefore, for sentient beings to take delight in it is not in accordance with reason.
If those within the True Dharma who believe in and delight in non-self find that the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is not what they cherish, they will feel no joy or pleasure therein.

This ālayavijñāna is grasped by sentient beings as their own internal self; therefore, even when born into a path of exclusively painful sensation, they do not wish for the cessation of the aggregates of suffering.
Because they are bound by self-love toward the ālayavijñāna, they never desire or seek its extinction.

Although sentient beings born from the fourth dhyāna upward do not delight in the feeling of sensual desire, within their ālayavijñāna, the love of self persists, following them without ever departing.

Furthermore, although those within the True Dharma aspire to and delight in non-self, thereby opposing the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi), they still possess self-love (*ātmasneha*) within the ālayavijñāna.
Establishing this consciousness by the name *ālaya* is the most excellent; this is called the establishment of the specific synonym *ālayavijñāna*. 2.
Second, the Chapter on Characteristics (*Lakṣaṇapariccheda*). Furthermore, how can the characteristics of this consciousness be understood?
These characteristics are briefly stated to be of three kinds:
first, the establishment of the self-characteristic; second, the establishment of the causal characteristic; and third, the establishment of the resultant characteristic.

Regarding the establishment of the self-characteristic: based on the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of all impure phenomena, that which serves as the support for their arising and maintains the seeds within its vessel is called the self-characteristic.

Regarding the establishment of the characteristic of cause (*hetu-lakṣaṇa*): this consciousness containing all seeds (*sarvabījaka-vijñāna*) constantly arises as the cause for the production of dharmas belonging to the impure category;

this is called the characteristic of cause. Regarding the establishment of the characteristic of fruit (*phala-lakṣaṇa*): this consciousness arises only through the beginningless habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of various dharmas belonging to the impure category; this is called the characteristic of fruit.
What dharma is called "habitual tendency" (*vāsanā*)?
What meaning does this term "habitual tendency" intend to reveal?
This dharma arises and ceases simultaneously with that [dharma] with which it is associated; subsequently, it transforms into the cause for the arising of that [dharma]. This is the meaning revealed.

For example, when sesame seeds are perfumed by flowers, the sesame and the flowers arise and perish simultaneously; as they arise repeatedly, the flowers become the cause for the arising of the fragrance in the sesame.

Likewise, when a person possesses conduct such as desire and has the latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) of desire and so forth, that mind arises and perishes simultaneously with the desire and the rest; as it arises repeatedly, it becomes the cause for the arising of the transformation of the mind.

If a person of great learning possesses the habitual tendencies of extensive study, their repeated reflection upon what has been heard arises and perishes together with the mind; these repeated occurrences serve as the cause for the arising of mental clarity.
Because these latencies (vāsanās) become firmly established through this process, such a person is said to be "one who upholds the Dharma.
This principle should be understood to apply to the ālayavijñāna in this manner.
Regarding the relationship between these defiled seeds and the ālayavijñāna:
they are not different because they do not possess separate substantial entities; yet, although they are difficult to distinguish due to such a union, they are not non-different.
The ālayavijñāna arises in this manner; at the time when it is perfumed, there is a superior capacity [in its nature] which is designated as "all seeds.
How can the ālayavijñāna and the defiled [dharmas] be mutual causes for one another simultaneously?
For example, the light of a lamp and its wick arise and burn simultaneously, each acting as a cause for the other at that very moment.
Or, like a bundle of reeds, they remain standing by virtue of supporting one another simultaneously.
It should be understood that the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) and the perfuming agents (*vāsana*) are likewise mutual causes for one another;
just as consciousness is the cause of defiled phenomena, so too are defiled phenomena the cause of consciousness.
Why is this? Because apart from these two dharmas, no other cause can be found.
How is it that perfuming (*vāsanā*), which is neither distinct nor manifold, can act as the productive cause for various phenomena that are distinct and manifold?
It is like a garment woven from many threads;
though the garment itself has no manifold colors, once it enters a dye-vat, various patterns subsequently become manifest upon it.
In this way, the ālayavijñāna is perfumed by various phenomena; at the time of perfuming, it is of a single nature and does not possess multiple kinds.
However, when the conditions for the arising of fruits—the vessel of defilement—manifest before it, then incalculable varieties of appearances manifest within the ālayavijñāna.
This dependent origination is most subtle and profound within the Mahāyāna.
To speak briefly, there are two kinds of dependent origination:
first, that which differentiates intrinsic nature; second, that which differentiates the agreeable and the disagreeable.

The arising of all phenomena based upon the ālayavijñāna is called the dependent origination of the imagined nature (*parikalpitasvabhāva-pratītyasamutpāda*), because it consists in the imagined nature of the causes and conditions of various phenomena.

Furthermore, there is the twelvefold dependent origination, which is called the "differentiation of the agreeable and the disagreeable," because it differentiates the various distinct causes for the arising of the agreeable and the disagreeable within the good and evil realms of existence.

If a person is deluded regarding the first dependent origination of the ālayavijñāna, they may either cling to intrinsic nature as the cause of birth and death, or cling to past actions, or cling to the transformations of Īśvara, or cling to the eightfold self, or cling to the absence of cause.
If one is deluded regarding the second dependent origination, one clings to a self as the agent and the experiencer.
It is like a group of many people born blind who have never seen an elephant; someone shows it to them so that they may touch and perceive it.
There were some blind men who, some touched its nose, some its tusks, some its ears, some its feet, some its tail, and some its back, and so forth.
Someone asked them, "What is the appearance of the elephant?
The blind men replied:
"The elephant is like the handle of a plow," or some said it was like a pestle; others said it was like a winnowing basket, or like a mortar, or like a broom, or like a mountain rock.

If a person does not understand these two kinds of dependent origination, being born blind through ignorance, they may claim that self-nature is the cause, or that past actions are the cause, or that the transformations of Īśvara are the cause, or that the eightfold self is the cause, or that there is no cause, or that there is an agent and an experiencer.

Because they do not understand the essence and characteristics of the ālayavijñāna, nor its causal characteristics, they produce various divergent explanations—just as those born blind who, failing to recognize the body of an elephant, offer various different descriptions.

To state the essence and characteristics of the ālayavijñāna briefly: it is the retributive consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) and the consciousness of all seeds (*sarvabījaka*). By means of this consciousness, all bodies within the three realms and all beings of the six destinies and four modes of birth are entirely subsumed.
To clarify this meaning, it is said in verse:
External and internal are not clearly established; Regarding these two, there are only conventional designations, As well as all that is ultimately real.
Perishing moment by moment, coexistent, following along until the limit of purification,
definitively observing causes and conditions, it is like drawing forth and manifesting its own fruit.
Firm, indeterminate, and capable of being perfumed, it is associated with that which perfumes.
If it were otherwise, it could not be perfumed; thus, this is said to be the characteristic of the substance of perfuming.
The six consciousnesses lack mutual association; their three distinctions are contradictory;
two moments do not coexist; and by extension, other births should be understood in the same way.
Furthermore, the internal seeds are both productive and sustaining causes;
they continue even after death and only then reach total extinction.
Unlike external seeds, internal seeds do not function in that way.
This meaning is revealed by two verses:
Without external perfuming, The seeds within would not exist;
Without the perfuming of hearing and so forth, It is illogical for the fruit to arise.
What has been done and what has not yet been done, loss and gain, as well as their opposites, are established through the internal and external; therefore, there is internal perfuming (*vāsanā*).

All other consciousnesses distinct from the *ālayavijñāna*—namely, the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*)—should be understood as existing in all places of birth and all realms of existence; these are called the "consciousnesses of experience" (*upabhogavijñāna*).
As stated in a verse of the *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya*:
"The first is called the consciousness of conditions (*ālambana-vijñapti*); The second is called the consciousness of sensation (*anubhava-vijñapti*);
To discern sensation is called discrimination (*vikalpa*), Which gives rise to mental factors such as volitional formations (*saṃskāra*)."
These two consciousnesses act as causes for one another, as stated in a verse from the *Mahāyānābhidharma*:
"All phenomena reside within the storehouse-consciousness, and the consciousness likewise resides within phenomena;
these two are mutual causes, and they are also constantly mutual effects."

If, within the first dependent origination, all phenomena and consciousness act as mutual causes and conditions for one another, then in the second dependent origination, what kind of condition do these phenomena constitute?
This is the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Furthermore, how many conditions can produce the six consciousnesses?
There are three conditions: namely, the dominant condition, the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
Thus, there are three types of dependent origination:

first, dependent origination that exhausts birth and death; second, dependent origination of the path of love and hatred; and third, dependent origination of enjoyment. These are fully endowed with the four conditions.
Chapter Three: Citation of Scriptural Authority (Āgamasaṃgrahapaṭala). This ālayavijñāna has already been established by way of its various names and its essential characteristics.
How is it to be known that this is the ālayavijñāna?
Because of these various names, the Tathāgata likewise spoke of the essence and characteristics [of consciousness], but did not speak of the arising consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*).

Apart from this ālayavijñāna established by means of these names and characteristics, neither the impure categories nor the pure categories would be established; that is, the impure category of afflictions (*kleśa*), the impure category of karma, the impure category of birth, the mundane pure category, and the supramundane pure category would all fail to be established.
How is it that the category of impurity consisting of afflictions is not established?
The seeds of perfuming produced by the root afflictions and the secondary afflictions cannot be established within the six consciousnesses.

Why is this? Visual consciousness arises and ceases simultaneously with the two categories of afflictions, both gross and subtle, such as desire; this visual consciousness is perfumed by these afflictions to establish seeds, whereas other consciousnesses are not so.

This visual consciousness has already ceased, or it is interrupted by other consciousnesses; thus, neither the perfuming nor its substratum can be apprehended. Since the visual consciousness of the preceding moment has already passed away and currently lacks any substantial entity, or because it is separated by other consciousnesses, it is impossible for desire to arise simultaneously with it from that which has already ceased and no longer exists—just as, for example, a karmic retribution cannot arise from past karma that has already been completely extinguished.
Furthermore, the perfuming of visual consciousness by desire and so forth cannot be established if they arise simultaneously. Why is this?
Because this seed cannot abide within the desire, as desire itself depends upon consciousness.

Furthermore, because desire is not stable and persists in a continuous stream, it cannot be perfumed by other consciousnesses; this is because their bases are distinct, and the remaining consciousnesses do not arise and perish simultaneously with it.
Like-kind [dharmas] cannot mutually perfume one another, because they do not arise and perish simultaneously.
Therefore, visual consciousness is not perfumed by the various great or small afflictions such as desire, nor is it perfumed by a consciousness of its own like-kind.
One should reflect upon visual consciousness in this manner, and the remaining consciousnesses should likewise be reflected upon.

Furthermore, if sentient beings fall from the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*) or above and take birth in a lower realm, their initial consciousness—tainted by gross and subtle afflictions—would have no seed at the time it arises.
Why is this? Because these afflictions and their habitual tendencies, along with their basis, have already passed away and are extinguished without remainder.
Furthermore, once the counteractive consciousness has arisen, all remaining mundane consciousnesses have been completely extinguished.
If the ālayavijñāna did not exist, it would be impossible for this counteractive consciousness to coexist with the seeds of both minor and major afflictions. Why is this so?
Because its nature is liberation; thus, an outflow-free mind cannot arise or cease simultaneously with the afflictions.

Furthermore, at a later time upon emerging from meditative absorption, when one correctly gives rise to a mundane mind, the latencies of the various afflictions have long since ceased and perished; thus, it would follow that the *manovijñāna* associated with the outflow of existence (*āsrava*) could arise even without seeds.
Therefore, apart from the ālayavijñāna, the defilement of afflictions cannot be established.
Furthermore, how is it that the defilement of karma cannot be established?
It is because the stage of consciousness arising conditioned by formative forces (*saṃskāra*) would have no basis for establishment.
If this principle did not exist, then the arising of existence conditioned by grasping would also lack validity; consequently, the defilement of karma would not be established.
Furthermore, how could the defilement of birth be established if this principle were not valid?
Because the linking of rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi*) would otherwise be impossible.

If a person falls from an unpeaceful state (*aśāntabhūmi*), they can only undergo rebirth when a defiled mental consciousness (*kliṣṭa-manovijñāna*) arises within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

This defiled consciousness ceases within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), and this consciousness then takes hold of the *kalala* in the mother’s womb, undergoing transformation and union to take birth.

If it were merely the mental consciousness that transforms into the support for the *kalala* and so forth, there would be no such principle as a distinct mental consciousness arising within the mother’s womb alongside that [transforming] mental consciousness.
Within the mother’s womb, two types of consciousness do not arise simultaneously; such a principle does not exist.

Furthermore, a transformed consciousness cannot be established as the support for the mental consciousness, because it is impure, because it takes objects for a long duration, and because its objects of cognition cannot be known.

If this consciousness has already undergone transformation, at that time the consciousness becomes the *kalala*. Is it because this consciousness is the seed of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-bīja*), or because other consciousnesses arise depending upon it? If you maintain that the transformed consciousness is called the "all-seed consciousness" (*sarvabījaka-vijñāna*), then it is precisely the *ālayavijñāna*; you are merely establishing it under a different name and calling it "consciousness" (*manovijñāna*).

If you maintain that the consciousness which serves as the support is itself the all-seed consciousness, then this supporting consciousness would become the cause of another [consciousness] by virtue of being its support.
In that case, if the supported consciousness were not the all-seed consciousness, it could not be designated as the "all-seed consciousness," and thus your position would be untenable.

Therefore, it is this consciousness that, upon entering a new birth, undergoes transformation to become the *kalala*; it is not the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Being both the fruit of maturation (*vipāka*) and the storehouse of all seeds (*sarvabījaka*), this principle is established.

Furthermore, once a sentient being has entered the womb, the ability to sustain the remaining sense faculties cannot be obtained apart from the retributive consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*). Why is this so?
The remaining consciousnesses necessarily have distinct supports that do not endure for long or remain stable.
Furthermore, if this material sense-faculty were not sustained by a grasping consciousness, it could not even come into being.

Moreover, this consciousness and name-and-form (nāmarūpa) depend upon one another, arising together like two bundles of reeds leaning against each other; [without such a support], this consciousness would not be established.

Furthermore, if one were apart from the resultant consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), the food of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*) would not be established for any sentient beings, whether seeking birth or already born. Why is this?

Because if one were apart from the resultant consciousness, it is not observed that any single consciousness among the visual consciousnesses and so forth has the capacity to function as the sustenance for sentient beings undergoing birth within the three realms.

If a person dies from this life and is born into a higher, tranquil realm (*śāntabhūmi*), they are reborn there by means of a distracted and defiled mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). In that case, it would follow that this defiled, distracted consciousness possesses seeds other than the retributive consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) within the tranquil realm; however, this proposition is untenable.

Furthermore, if beings are born in the formless realm, apart from the resultant consciousness that contains all seeds, then when a defiled mind or a wholesome mind arises, it would lack both its seed and its support; thus, both the defiled and wholesome consciousnesses could not be established.
If one gives rise to an untainted mind within the formless realm, all remaining mundane minds have already ceased, and one should thus abandon this path.
If sentient beings are born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and give rise to a mind of the sphere of nothingness or an untainted mind, they immediately relinquish both spheres.

Why is this? Because the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) is a supramundane mind; thus, the path of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) is not its support, the path of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) is also not its support, and even the direct course toward nirvāṇa is not its support.

Furthermore, if a person who has already performed wholesome or unwholesome karma were to cast off their life-force while separated from the *ālayavijñāna*, the gradual process of the body’s temperature becoming cold, whether from the top down or from the bottom up, could not be established.
Therefore, the arising of defilement cannot be established apart from the retributive consciousness that contains all seeds (*sarvabījaka-vipākavijñāna*).
How is it that the pure categories of the mundane world would not be established?

If sentient beings have not yet abandoned desire and have not yet attained the mind of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), they first give rise to wholesome minds of the desire realm to seek liberation from desire, practicing the contemplative mind of the desire realm.

Because this preparatory mind (*prayoga-citta*) of the desire realm does not arise and cease simultaneously with the mind of the form realm, it is not perfumable; therefore, the wholesome mind of the desire realm is not the seed of the wholesome mind of the form realm.

Past consciousnesses of the form realm are separated from the present by immeasurable other births and distinct mental states; therefore, they cannot be established as the seeds of tranquil consciousness, as they no longer exist.

Therefore, this principle is established: namely, that the maturation-consciousness (vipākavijñāna), which contains all seeds and consists of the tranquil mind of the form realm (rūpadhātu), is established as the causal condition (hetu-pratyaya) through successive transmission, while this preparatory wholesome mind (prayoga-kuśala-citta) is established as the dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya).
In this manner, this principle should be understood to apply to all stages of freedom from desire (*vairāgya-bhūmi*).
Thus, the meaning of the worldly category of purification (*laukika-vyavadāna*) cannot be established apart from the retributive consciousness containing all seeds (*sarvabījaka-vipākavijñāna*).
How is it that the supramundane category of purity cannot be established apart from the ālayavijñāna?
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, has said:
"From hearing the voice of another and from one’s own correct reflection—through these two causes, right view arises."

This hearing of another's voice and correct reflection cannot permeate the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*), the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*), or both the ear- and mental consciousnesses. Why is this?

When a person understands the Dharma as they have heard it and correctly reflects upon it, at that time the ear-consciousness cannot arise, nor can the mental consciousness arise, because what is heard is processed by other distracted and discursive consciousnesses.

If [the subsequent consciousness] arises in association with correct reflection (*samyak-saṃkalpa*), that preceding mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) has long since ceased and perished; since the perfuming by what was heard and the co-perfuming have already vanished, how can the subsequent consciousness arise later with the prior consciousness as its seed?

Furthermore, the worldly mind associated with right reflection and the supramundane pure mind associated with right view can never arise or cease together; therefore, this worldly mind is not perfumed by the pure mind.
Since there would be no perfuming, it could not become a supramundane seed.
Therefore, apart from the resultant consciousness containing all seeds, the supramundane pure mind could also not be established.
Why is this? Because within this [consciousness], the latencies (*vāsanā*) produced by hearing and reflection lack the capacity to encompass the seeds of supramundane latencies.

How could the retributive consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), which possesses all seeds, become the cause of the impure category, while simultaneously acting as the cause for the pure supramundane mind that serves as the antidote to defilement?
This supramundane mind has never been produced or cultivated in the past; therefore, it certainly lacks any perfuming.
If there is no perfuming, from what cause does this supramundane mind arise?
You should now respond:
Since the supramundane mind arises with the seeds of the correct hearing-perfuming that flows from the most pure dharma-realm,
is this perfuming of the wisdom of hearing of the same nature as the ālayavijñāna, or is it of a different nature?
If it were of the nature of the ālayavijñāna, how could it constitute the seeds that serve as its antidote?
If it were not of the same nature, upon what dharma would these seeds of the wisdom derived from hearing rely?

Up until the stage of the Buddhas' unsurpassed enlightenment, this [wisdom] arises from the perfuming of the wisdom of hearing; wherever it may abide, it co-arises with the resultant maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), just like water and milk.
This perfuming by hearing is not the fundamental consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), for it has already become the seed that serves as the antidote to that consciousness.
Within this process, medium-grade perfuming arises based on inferior-grade perfuming, and superior-grade perfuming arises based on medium-grade perfuming.
Why is this? Because of the repeated application of hearing, reflection, and cultivation (*śruta-cintā-bhāvanā*).

This perfuming by hearing (*śruta-vāsanā*), whether it be of inferior, middling, or superior grade, should be known as the seed of the *dharmakāya*. It arises as the antidote to the *ālayavijñāna*; therefore, it is not included within the nature of the *ālaya*. Although it is a worldly phenomenon, it gives rise to supramundane consciousness because it flows forth from the most pure supramundane *dharmadhātu*.

Why is this? Because when this seed of supramundane pure mind has not yet arisen, it serves as the antidote to all active afflictions (*paryavasthāna*), the antidote to rebirth in all evil destinies, and the antidote to the decay of all unwholesome conduct; it is capable of drawing forth the continuum so that it may be born in such a place, where one may encounter and serve the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in accordance with the Dharma.

Although this perfuming by hearing is a mundane phenomenon, it should be understood that when first attained by a bodhisattva practicing contemplation, this dharma is subsumed under the Dharma-body (dharmakāya).
If it is attained by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, it is subsumed under the Liberation-body (vimuktikāya).
This perfuming by hearing is not the ālayavijñāna; it is subsumed under the dharmakāya and the vimuktikāya.

In this manner, as it gradually increases through the stages of inferior, middling, and superior, the retributive consciousness (vipākavijñāna) correspondingly and gradually diminishes, and the basis is thereby transformed.

If the transformation occurs through total reliance [on the fundamental consciousness], then the resultant consciousness that possesses seeds would be devoid of seeds, and everything would be completely exhausted.

If the fundamental consciousness and the non-fundamental consciousness arise and perish together, like milk and water mixed, how can it be that the fundamental consciousness ceases while the non-fundamental consciousness does not?
It is, for example, like a swan drinking milk from water.

Just as in the world, when one becomes free from desire, the latencies (*vāsanā*) of the non-quiescent stages are extinguished and the latencies of the quiescent stages increase, such that the meaning of the worldly transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) is accomplished; so too is it with the supramundane transformation of the basis.

If a person enters the meditative absorption of the cessation of mind, it is taught that consciousness does not depart from the body; therefore, the resultant consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) must likewise remain non-departed from the body during that absorption. Why is this so?
The attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) is not the antidote to this consciousness. How is this known?
If one were to emerge from this meditative state, consciousness should not arise again.
Why is this? Because once the continuity of this retributive consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) has been severed, it cannot arise again unless it relies upon the moment of rebirth.
If someone claims that there is a mind during the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), what such a person says does not constitute a [valid] mind.

Why is this? Because its definition cannot be established; because the characteristics of liberation and its object cannot be apprehended; because it would entail the fault of being associated with wholesome roots; because it would not be associated with the unwholesome or the indeterminate; because it would entail the fault of the arising of perception and feeling; because there must necessarily be contact when the three [faculties] come together; because it would have efficacy toward other meditative concentrations; because the mere cessation of perception is a defect; because it would entail the fault of the arising of mental attention, faith, and other wholesome roots; because it is impossible to extract that which depends while remaining apart from its basis; because there is a supporting analogy; and because, unlike the case where all formations are not thus, it is not the case that all formations are like this.
If someone maintains that the sequential arising of form and mind constitutes the seeds of all phenomena,
this position is incorrect. Why is this so?
Since there is already the aforementioned fault, there is furthermore another distinct error.

As for this distinct error: if a person were to fall from the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*) or emerge from the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), that which is maintained here would not be established;
nor could the final mind of an Arhat be established.
If one were to exclude the condition of immediate succession (*samanantarapratyaya*), this [mental] apprehension would not be established.

Likewise, if one were to exclude the retributive consciousness containing all seeds (*sarvabījaka-vipākavijñāna*), neither the pure nor the impure categories could be established. Therefore, it should be known with faith that the existence of this mind is logically proven.
Based on the characteristics previously explained, I shall now further compose a verse:
When a bodhisattva relies upon the wholesome consciousness, They then depart from the other five consciousnesses;
Since there is no remaining mind for the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), By what means is this accomplished?
If the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) were the antidote, it would not be established because it is not a cessation;
since there would be no distinction between cause and effect, there would be a logical fault regarding cessation.
If one were to assert that the transformation of the basis consists of the absence of seeds and the absence of dharmas, [it would be untenable].
Because duality does not exist, the meaning of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) is not established.
Chapter Four: On Differentiation. What are the differentiations of this *ālayavijñāna*?
To speak briefly, there are either three or four types of distinctions.

As for the three types, they arise from the differences among three kinds of perfuming (*vāsanā*): namely, the distinctions between the perfuming of verbal expression, the perfuming of the view of self, and the perfuming of the constituent parts of existence (*bhavāṅga*).
The four kinds are: the distinction of production, the distinction of retribution, the distinction of causal characteristics, and the distinction of phenomenal appearances.
The distinction of production refers to the new arising of perfuming (*vāsanā*).
If this were not so, the principle that consciousness arises conditioned by formations (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*) arises conditioned by grasping (*upādāna*) would not be established.
As for the differentiation of karmic fruition: based on these formations, these dharmas ripen within the six realms of existence.
If this did not exist, the arising of all phenomena at the time of future rebirth would be impossible.
As for the distinction of objective conditions (*ālambana-nimitta*), within this mind there are signs that can give rise to the grasping of a self (*ātma-grāha*).
If this [consciousness] did not exist, the apprehension of the object characterized as a self within other states of mind would be untenable.

As for the distinction of its characteristics: this consciousness possesses both common characteristics and non-common characteristics; it possesses the characteristic of seeds that do not produce rebirth and the characteristic of seeds that do produce rebirth.
The common characteristic (*sādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa*) refers to the seeds of the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*).
The uncommon characteristic (*asādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa*) refers to the seeds of the individual internal bases (*ādhyātmika-āyatana*).
Furthermore, the common characteristic refers to the seeds of birth that is without sensation (*anupabhoga-janman*).
As for the unique characteristics (*asādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa*), these are the seeds for the production of experience with sensation.
When their antidote arises, the unique objects of that antidote are extinguished.

Regarding the shared seeds within consciousness, which are maintained by the conceptualizations of others, they are purified through right view; this is, for example, like a practitioner of meditation who, regarding a single type of object, establishes various perceptions according to his mind through various aspirations and various observations.
Regarding this, a verse is spoken:
Difficult to extinguish and difficult to unravel, They are called the shared fetters (*sādhāraṇa-saṃyojana*).
The mental states of those who practice contemplation differ; Due to the magnitude of their characteristics, they appear as external.
As long as pure beings have not ceased, one perceives purity therein;
by perceiving purity through the Buddha, one accomplishes a pure buddha-field.
Furthermore, there is another verse:
Various vows and views are accomplished by the practitioner;
because they are established according to their own intentions regarding a single class of objects,
and because various perceptions are thus established, that which is apprehended is nothing but consciousness.
This is the non-common seed for the arising of sensation within the differentiation of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
If this did not exist, the conditions for the arising of the world of sentient beings would not be established.
This is the common seed for the arising of non-sensation within the *ālayavijñāna*.
If this were absent, the conditions for the arising of the receptacle world would not be established.
Furthermore, there are consciousnesses characterized by heaviness and rigidity (*dausthulya*) and consciousnesses characterized by subtlety and lightness.
Consciousness characterized by heaviness and rigidity refers to the seeds of the two types of afflictions, both gross and subtle.
The subtle, light characteristic of consciousness refers to the seeds of all contaminated (*sāsrava*) wholesome dharmas.
If this did not exist, the distinction between the bases that possess superior capacity and those that lack superior capacity—arising from the fruits of prior karma—could not be established.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna): that characterized by being appropriated (*upātta*) and that characterized by not being appropriated (*anupātta*).
That which is characterized by being appropriated refers to the consciousness of the seeds of good and evil whose retributive fruits have already matured.

That which is characterized by not being appropriated refers to the seeds of the perfuming of names and phrases (*nāma-pada-vāsanā*), because they are the seeds from which conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) arises throughout immeasurable time.

If this consciousness did not exist, the principle of the exhaustion of experience through the cause of the two types of karma—wholesome and unwholesome—and their resulting retributions would not be established; furthermore, the arising of the habitual perfuming of names and phrases at the moment of initial birth could not be established either.
Furthermore, there is the characteristic of analogy.
Consciousness is like a magical illusion, a mirage, a dream, a visual impairment, and so forth; the primary consciousness resembles these phenomena.
If this did not exist, because it is the seed of false discrimination, this consciousness would not constitute the causal condition for perversion.
Furthermore, there are characteristics of being complete or incomplete:

if sentient beings are bound by all fetters, they possess the characteristic of completeness; if they have attained worldly detachment from desire, they possess the characteristic of impairment; if they are śrāvakas in training (*śaikṣa*) or various bodhisattvas, they possess the characteristic of partial cessation and detachment; and if they are arhats, pratyekabuddhas, or tathāgatas, they possess the characteristic of complete cessation and detachment.

Why is this? Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas extinguish only the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), whereas the Tathāgata extinguishes both the obstacle of afflictions and the obstacle to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
If this [obstacle to knowledge] did not exist, the gradual extinction of the afflictions could not be accomplished.
For what reason are the karmic fruits of the two dharmas—wholesome and unwholesome—exclusively non-obscured neutral?
This neutral nature is not incompatible with arising simultaneously with both wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, whereas the wholesome and unwholesome dharmas themselves are mutually contradictory.
If the fruition were established as having the nature of good or evil, there would be no means to attain liberation from afflictions.
Furthermore, because there would be no means to give rise to either virtue or affliction, there would be neither liberation nor bondage.
Because these two meanings do not exist, the retributive consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) is necessarily of the nature of being non-obscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*). 2.
The Second Chapter: On the Superior Characteristics of What is to be Known (*Jñeyalakṣaṇa*), Part One. Thus has been explained the basis of what is to be known (*jñeyāśraya*).
How should the superior characteristics be known?
One should know the superior characteristics.
Briefly stated, these characteristics to be known are of three kinds:
First, the characteristic of the dependent nature; second, the characteristic of the imagined nature; third, the characteristic of the perfected nature.

Regarding the characteristic of the dependent nature: it consists of the various distinctions among the consciousnesses subsumed under false discrimination, which take the fundamental consciousness as their seed.

What constitutes their differentiation? It refers to the body-consciousness, the consciousness of the self as a body, the consciousness of the experiencer, the consciousness of the object to be experienced, the consciousness of the actual experience, the consciousness of time, the consciousness of number, the consciousness of place, the consciousness of speech, the consciousness of the distinction between self and other, and the consciousness of birth and death within the two paths of good and evil.

The body-consciousness, the consciousness of the self, the consciousness of the experiencer, the consciousness of the object to be experienced, the consciousness of the actual experience, the consciousness of time, the consciousness of number, the consciousness of place, and the consciousness of verbal expression—these various consciousnesses arise from the seeds perfumed by verbal expression.
The consciousness that discriminates between self and others arises from the seeds of the habitual perfuming of the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*).
The consciousness of birth and death within the two paths of good and evil arises from the seeds of the habitual perfuming of the existence-element (*bhavāṅga*).
By means of such consciousnesses, the false discrimination characterized by the dependent nature—which is comprised of all realms, paths, and afflictions—is manifested.

These consciousnesses, being comprised within false discrimination, have representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*) as their essence; they are the basis for the manifestation of non-existent, false objects. This is called the characteristic of the dependent nature.

Regarding the characteristic of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*): in reality there are no external objects; it is only the substance of consciousness that manifests as objects. This is called the characteristic of the imagined nature. Regarding the characteristic of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*):

this refers to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) in which these objective characteristics are eternally non-existent, yet this [perfected nature] itself is not non-existent. This is called the characteristic of the perfected nature.

By means of the body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*), the consciousness of the self (*dehavijñāna*), and the consciousness of the experiencer (*bhoktṛvijñāna*), one should know that the six internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*), such as the eye, are subsumed.
By means of the consciousness of what is to be experienced (*vedanīyavijñāna*), one should know that the six external bases (*bāhyāyatana*), such as form, are subsumed.

By means of the consciousness of correct reception (*samyag-upalabdhi-vijñāna*), one should understand that it subsumes the six consciousness-elements (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna-dhātu*) beginning with the eye. With such consciousness as the basis, all other consciousnesses are its various manifestations (*viśeṣa*).
Thus, these various consciousnesses are *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only), because they lack objects such as external dust (*rajas*).

For example, in dreams and the like, apart from all external objects, there is exclusively consciousness-only; various objects such as forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, houses, forests, lands, and mountains appear as they truly are, yet not a single one of these objects exists as a reality.
By means of this analogy, one should understand that in all cases there is only consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*).
By the phrase "and so forth," one should understand the analogies of magical illusions, mirages, and visual impairments such as cataracts.
If one awakens from the perception of objects seen by others, then in all places there is only consciousness, just like the objects in a dream.
Just as when a person awakens from a dream, they discern that the dream-objects were merely consciousness, why is it not the same upon waking from this [present] state?
It is not that this principle does not exist.
If a person has already attained the awakening to the wisdom of *tathatā*, this awakening is certainly present.
It is, for example, like a person who is still in the midst of a dream and has not yet awakened; in such a state, this awakening does not arise.
If a person has already awakened, only then does this awakening exist.
Likewise, if a person has not yet attained the awakening of the wisdom of *tathatā*, they do not possess this awakening;
if they have already attained the awakening of the wisdom of *tathatā*, they necessarily possess this awakening.
If a person has not yet attained the realization of the wisdom of *tathatā*, how can they give rise to inferential knowledge (*anumāna*) regarding *vijñaptimātratā*?
It is through sacred scripture (*āgama*) and logical reasoning (*yukti*) that such inference may be achieved.
Regarding the sacred teaching, as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, stated in the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra*:
"O Son of the Buddha!
The three realms consist of nothing but consciousness."
Furthermore, as stated in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, at that time the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya asked the Buddha, the World-Honored One: "World-Honored One,
is this objective referent of the concentrated mind distinct from the mind, or is it not distinct from the mind?"
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, said:
"Maitreya, it is not different from the mind."
Why is this? I teach that there is only consciousness; these objective realms of form-appearances are manifested by consciousness.
Maitreya Bodhisattva said:
World-Honored One!
If the objective sphere of meditative concentration is not different from the concentrated mind in its form and characteristics,
how can this consciousness take that very same consciousness as its object?
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, said: "Maitreya!
There is no dharma that can grasp another dharma."
Although it cannot be grasped, this consciousness arises as a transformation that manifests like an object.
It is, for example, like seeing one's face by relying on a mirror and thinking, "I see my reflection"; yet this reflection appears as something distinct from the face itself.
The concentrated mind is likewise; it manifests appearing as if it were an external object, which is to say, as something distinct from the concentrated mind itself.
By means of this scripture (*āgama*) and the reasoning established thereby, the principle of *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only) is revealed.

Why is this so? At that time, when the practitioner’s mind is precisely within meditative observation, if they perceive the pervasive forms of colors such as blue or yellow, they see only their own mind and do not see any external objects such as blue or yellow colors.
By this principle, among all forms of consciousness, a bodhisattva should apply such inferential reasoning regarding representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*).
Regarding consciousnesses of blue, yellow, and so forth, these are not recollective consciousnesses (*smṛtivijñāna*), because the objects are perceived as being present before one.

In the two stages of hearing and reflection, the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) retains [the teachings]; this consciousness takes past objects as its objective condition and arises appearing as those past objects.
Therefore, the principle of Vijñaptimātra (consciousness-only) is established.

From this inference, it is known that if a bodhisattva has not yet attained the awakening to the wisdom of *tathatā*, they can still attain inferential knowledge regarding the principle of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*).

These various forms of consciousness have been explained previously; for example, like magical illusions or dreams, within them the principle of consciousness-only is established for the visual consciousness and the other sensory cognitions.
If the consciousnesses of the eye, forms, and so forth possess form, how can the meaning of "consciousness-only" (vijñapti-mātra) be perceived?
These consciousnesses should be understood as before, through both scripture (āgama) and reasoning (yukti).
If form were consciousness, how could it manifest as resembling form?
How could it persist in a continuous stream, remaining stable and similar from beginning to end?
This is because it serves as the basis for afflictions such as inversion.
If it were not so, the inversion of non-meaning into meaning could not be established.
If there were no inversion regarding meaning, the two kinds of afflictions—the obstruction of the defilements and the obstruction to knowledge—could not be established.
If the two obstacles did not exist, the category of the pure (viśuddha-pakṣa) could not be established either.
Therefore, it is credible that the various consciousnesses arise in this manner as a reality.
Regarding this, a verse is spoken:
The cause of confusion and the essence of confusion consist of material consciousness and immaterial consciousness.
If the preceding consciousness does not exist, the subsequent consciousness cannot arise.

How is it that body-consciousness, the consciousness of the self, the consciousness of the experiencer, the consciousness of the object to be experienced, and the consciousness of the actual experience arise in all places of birth, mutually and closely conjoined?
Because it is manifested through the full accomplishment of birth. How is it that the consciousnesses of the world and so forth arise with various distinctions as previously described?

Because the continuity of beginningless birth and death is uninterrupted; because they are comprised within the immeasurable realms of sentient beings; because they are comprised within the immeasurable receptacle worlds; because they are comprised within the immeasurable mutual manifestations of activities; because they are comprised within the immeasurable distinctions of inclusion and enjoyment; because they are comprised within the immeasurable karmic fruits of enjoyment, such as love and hatred; and because they are comprised within the immeasurable distinctions of the realization of birth and death.
How are these various consciousnesses correctly analyzed so as to establish the principle of *vijñaptimātratā* (consciousness-only)?

Briefly stated, there are three characteristics by which all consciousnesses are established as consciousness-only: because there is only the measure of consciousness and no external objects exist; because... [text continues] ...because... [text continues]. Thus, through these three characteristics, all consciousnesses are proven to be consciousness-only.
There are only two [factors], namely the characteristic (*nimitta*) and the vision (*darśana*), because they are subsumed under consciousness (*vijñāna*);
and by virtue of their diversity, they are subsumed under the arising of characteristics.
What is the meaning of this?
All these consciousnesses are devoid of external objects; therefore, they are established as *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only).

They possess both the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*): the various consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, take form and other objects as their image-part, while those same visual and other consciousnesses take the consciousnesses themselves as their seeing-part;

furthermore, the mental consciousness takes all consciousnesses, from the visual consciousness up to the mental-object consciousness, as its image-part, while the mental consciousness itself serves as its seeing-part.

Why is this so? Because the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is capable of conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*), and because it arises as if appearing as the objects (*viṣaya*) of all [other] consciousnesses.
Regarding this, a verse is spoken:

The various teachers explain that this mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises in accordance with various bases and thus receives various names—such as when one enters the stages of "representation-only" (*vijñaptimātra*), "the two [grasps]," or the various views of persons;

likewise during the stage of penetrating *vijñaptimātra* and the stage of suppressing and abandoning consciousness. It is, for example, like how the action of volition (*cetanā-karman*) receives the names of bodily and vocal actions.
This consciousness, arising upon all bases, manifests various appearances in the likeness of two kinds of phenomena:
first, it appears in the likeness of objects; second, it appears in the likeness of discrimination.

In all places, there is an appearance resembling tangibility; if one is in a realm possessing form, the mental consciousness arises in dependence upon the body, just as the material sense-faculties arise in dependence upon the body.
In this regard, a verse is spoken:
Far-reaching and traveling alone, Bodyless, dwelling in the hollow of space;
Taming that which is difficult to tame— Thus one is liberated from the bonds of Māra.
As the Sūtra says:
"The objects apprehended by each of these five faculties, such as the eye, are grasped by the mental consciousness; the discriminating mental consciousness serves as the cause for their arising."
Furthermore, there is another explanation: within the analysis of the twelve bases (*āyatana*), this collection of the six consciousnesses is called the mind base (*manāyatana*).

In this context, the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is established as the object-consciousness (*arthavijñāna*), while all other consciousnesses therein are called the representation-consciousness (*nimittavijñāna*).
The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and the supporting consciousness (*āśrayavijñāna*) should be known as the "seeing-consciousness" (*darśanavijñāna*). Why is this?

Because this object-aspect consciousness (*nimittavijñāna*) is the cause for the arising of seeing; since it manifests as if it were an external object, it performs the function of being the basis for the arising of seeing.
In this way, these various consciousnesses establish the nature of Vijñapti-mātra (consciousness-only).
How is it that objects manifest before us, yet we know them to be non-existent?
As the Blessed One, the Buddha, has said:
If a bodhisattva is endowed with four dharmas, they are able to seek out and enter into the fact that all consciousnesses are devoid of external objects. What are these four?

First, knowing the characteristics of contradictory consciousnesses; for example, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and devas perceive the same objective sphere differently due to the diversity of their consciousnesses.
Second, because one perceives that consciousness has no objective realm, as in the case of [consciousness] regarding the past, the future, dreams, reflections, or atoms.

Third, because one knows that it would follow that there is no error even in the absence of effort; for example, if consciousness were to arise in relation to an object when that object truly exists, it would not be erroneous and would not depend on effort, since it would know the object as it truly is.
Fourth, it is because the meaning is known in accordance with the three types of wisdom. How is this so?
All noble ones enter meditative equipoise and attain mastery over the mind; by virtue of their mastery over aspiration and resolve, various objects appear exactly as they have willed or resolved.
If a practitioner has already attained śamatha and applies the preparatory practice of dharma-contemplation, because only the appearance of the object of thought manifests;
and if a person has attained non-conceptual wisdom and has not yet emerged from non-conceptual contemplation, because no sensory objects manifest at all.

Because the meanings of the objects and so forth accord with the three types of wisdom, and because the meaning of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*) has been established by the preceding citations of proof, it is known that consciousness-only is devoid of external objects.
Within this, there are six verses that further clarify the aforementioned meaning.
This verse will be explained in detail later in the section on the training in wisdom (*jñāna-śikṣā*), concerning such beings as hungry ghosts, animals, and humans.
