Part Two of the Second Chapter: "The Superior Characteristics of What Should Be Known. If the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is defined as that which is the basis for the manifestation of consciousness appearing as objects, in what sense is it established as "dependent"?
For what reason is it called "dependent" (*paratantra*)?
Because it arises from seeds of its own habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*), it is bound to causes and conditions and lacks independence.
Furthermore, because it has no power to arise once a single moment has passed and must abide by itself [only for that duration], it is called "dependent."

If the nature of discrimination (parikalpita-svabhāva) is that which appears as an object while being entirely non-existent in its dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva), how can it be established as discrimination?
For what reason and by what conditions is it called "discrimination"?
The consciousness that discriminates immeasurable appearances is called "discrimination" because it is the cause for the arising of inversion;
since it lacks intrinsic characteristics and perceives only discrimination, it is termed "discrimination."
If the nature of reality (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) has as its characteristic that the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) is eternally non-existent, how does it become "reality"?
For what reason and by what conditions is it called "reality"?
It becomes reality because it is as it is and not otherwise.
Because it accomplishes the pure realm, because it is the most excellent among all wholesome dharmas, and because it is accomplished in the ultimate sense, it is called "the real.
Furthermore, if there is the conceptualizer and that which is conceptualized, the nature of conceptualization is established.
In this context, what dharma is called "discrimination" (vikalpa)?
What dharma is that which is discriminated?
And what dharma is termed "the nature of discrimination" (parikalpita-svabhāva)?
Mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is discrimination, because it possesses three kinds of discrimination.

Why is this? This consciousness has the verbal habitual tendencies as its seeds, as well as the verbal habitual tendencies of all [other] consciousnesses as its seeds; therefore, this arising occurs through boundless discrimination. All discrimination in every respect is merely called "discrimination," and thus it is designated as discrimination.
This dependent nature is merely that which is conceptualized.
Because it is the cause that establishes the dependent nature as being conceptualized, it is termed "the nature of conceptualization" (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) herein.
How does conceptualization perform its reckoning?
This dependent nature is merely like the appearances of the myriad things; upon what object does it depend?
What characteristics does it grasp?
How is it perceived and seen?
What is dependent origination?
What is verbal expression?
What is conceptual proliferation?

Based on objects such as names and so forth, within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), one discriminates by means of four factors: through attachment to signs; through the arising of views based on definitive judgment; through the causal origination of discursive thought and verbal expression; and through the superimposition (*samāropa*) that conceives objects to be substantially real when they are in fact non-existent in relation to the four types of verbal expression, such as views. It is by these causes that one is able to discriminate.
What are these three natures?
Are they different from others, or not different?
One should say that they are neither different nor not different.
From another perspective, the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) is called "dependent" (paratantra).
From another perspective, it constitutes the "imagined" (parikalpita).
From another perspective, it constitutes the "perfected" or "real" (pariniṣpanna).
In what sense is this termed "dependent" (paratantra) from another perspective?
It is because it is bound to others by virtue of its seeds of perfuming (vāsanā).
Furthermore, in what sense is this considered "discrimination" (vikalpa)?

This dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) serves as the cause for conceptual construction (*parikalpa*); because it is that which is conceptually constructed, it constitutes conceptual construction.
Furthermore, in what sense does this constitute the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*)?
This dependent nature may constitute the perfected nature because the object as it is conceptually constructed does not exist in reality in that manner.
Furthermore, by what principle does this single consciousness constitute the various appearances of all forms of consciousness?

Because the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) possesses the various appearances of the other evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), and because these [evolving consciousnesses] arise based on those appearances.
How many kinds of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) are there? Briefly stated, there are two:

first, that which is bound to the seeds of perfuming (*vāsanā-bīja*); second, that which is bound to the non-establishment of the nature of the pure and impure categories. Therefore, it is called "dependent" by virtue of these two types of bondage.
The nature of conceptualization also has two types:
first, by way of the intrinsic nature of conceptualization; second, by way of the differentiation of conceptualization.
The nature of reality also has two types:
First, accomplishment through intrinsic nature; second, accomplishment through purity.
Furthermore, when further differentiated, there are four types:
first, differentiation of intrinsic nature; second, differentiation of distinctions; third, with awareness; and fourth, without awareness.
Those with discernment (*sa-vitarka*) are able to differentiate the conceptualizations of sentient beings regarding names and expressions;
those without discernment (*a-vitarka*) are unable to differentiate the conceptualizations of sentient beings regarding names and expressions.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of conceptualization (*vikalpa*):
First, there is the discrimination of the intrinsic nature of an object based on its name, as in: "This name refers to this object.
Second, there is the discrimination of the intrinsic nature of a name based on its object, as in: "This object belongs to this name."
Third, based on names, one discriminates the intrinsic nature of names, as when one discriminates a name whose meaning has not yet been understood.
Fourth, based on meanings, one discriminates the intrinsic nature of meanings, as when one discriminates a meaning whose name has not yet been understood.
Fifth, based on the two types of discrimination, one distinguishes the two natures: for example, this name [corresponds to] this object; what is the object and what is the name?
If all forms of discrimination are subsumed, there are further ten kinds:
first, fundamental discrimination, which refers to the root consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
Second is the discrimination of characteristics, which refers to consciousnesses such as those of form (*rūpa*).
Third is the discrimination of manifestation based on a support, which refers to consciousnesses that have supports such as the eye.

Fourth is the discrimination of transformation of characteristics, which refers to transformations such as aging; feelings such as suffering and pleasure; afflictions such as desire and resentment; transformations of time and season; and transformations of the hells and the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Fifth is the discrimination based on manifesting transformation, which refers to the arising of discrimination regarding transformation as previously described.
Sixth is discrimination induced by others, which refers to the discrimination arising from hearing categories of non-orthodox teachings or hearing categories of orthodox teachings.
Seventh is improper discrimination (*ayoniśovikalpa*), which refers to the discrimination of those outside the True Dharma regarding what is not of the nature of the True Dharma.
Eighth is proper discrimination (*yoniśovikalpa*), which refers to the discrimination of those within the True Dharma regarding what is of the nature of the True Dharma as heard from the True Dharma.

Ninth is the discrimination of adherence to views, which refers to the category of improper mental attention (ayoniśomanasikāra) that has the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) as its root and is associated with the sixty-two views.
The ten types of discursive distraction refer to the ten kinds of conceptualization of a bodhisattva:

the distraction of non-existence of characteristics, the distraction of existence of characteristics, the distraction of superimposition, the distraction of denial, the distraction of grasping at unity, the distraction of grasping at difference, the distraction of generality, the distraction of particularity, the distraction of conceiving an object according to its name, and the distraction of conceiving a name according to its object.

To counteract these ten types of distracted conceptualization, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has taught within all the Prajñāpāramitā teachings that non-conceptual wisdom can counteract these ten types of distraction;
one should know that this fully embodies the meaning of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras.
As it is said in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:
"How does a bodhisattva practice the perfection of wisdom? Śāriputra!"

This bodhisattva truly exists as a bodhisattva, yet does not perceive a bodhisattva, does not perceive the name "bodhisattva," does not perceive the *prajñāpāramitā*, does not perceive practicing, nor does he perceive not-practicing; he does not perceive form, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
Why is this? Form is empty by its own nature; it is not through the emptiness of emptiness that one perceives form as empty.
It is not that form is different from emptiness or that non-form is different from emptiness; rather, form is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself form.
Why is this? Śāriputra, these are merely names.

What is called "form" is its own nature: it is without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purity; it is a designation established in relation to the conceptual differentiation of all phenomena.

Because adventitious names are provisionally established, one speaks of all phenomena according to their suchness (tathatā); yet, in accordance with such speech, one gives rise to attachment to this or that. A bodhisattva does not perceive any of these names; if they do not perceive them, they do not give rise to attachment.
Just as one contemplates form, so too should one contemplate up to consciousness in this same manner.
Based on these words from the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, one should reflect accordingly upon the ten types of analytical meanings.
If, by this distinct intention, the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) is established as having three natures, what are these three natures?
There are three distinct natures; they do not become intermingled, nor is there any sense of their being intermingled.
By this principle, this nature constitutes the dependent (paratantra), but it does not constitute the imagined (parikalpita) or the perfected (pariniṣpanna) by virtue of this.
By this principle, this nature constitutes the imagined, but it does not constitute the dependent or the perfected by virtue of this.
By this principle, this nature (the perfected nature) is established as the ultimate reality; it is not by this that the dependent and the imagined natures are established.
How is it known that this dependent nature, which appears as phenomena through the imagined nature, does not share the same substance as the imagined nature?
Because knowledge regarding an object should not arise prior to its being named.
If the essence of a phenomenon (*dharmatā*) were identical with its name, this would contradict the fact that names are manifold.
If the name were identical with the object, then since names are many, the objects would necessarily become many; thus, this would contradict the nature of the object itself.
Because names are indeterminate and their referents are conflated, these meanings are contradictory.
Regarding this, a verse is spoken:
Before the name, there is no cognition; Names are manifold and indeterminate.
The establishment of meaning proceeds through identity, whereas multiplicity and diversity are contradictory.
Phenomena have no manifestation yet appear as if they exist; they are without defilement yet possess purity.
Therefore, they are likened to magical illusions and also compared to space.
How is it that while things appear in this way, they do not exist in reality, yet the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) exists in all its aspects?
If the dependent nature were non-existent, the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) would also be non-existent; thus, [the claim of] universal non-existence would not be established.
If the dependent nature and the perfected nature did not exist, there would be the fault of there being neither the category of defilement nor the category of purification.
Since these two categories are known not to be non-existent, it follows that not everything is non-existent.
Regarding this, a verse is spoken:
If the dependent nature did not exist, The perfected nature would also not exist;
Then there would eternally be no two categories, Namely, the defiled and the pure.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have taught the *Vibhāṣā-sūtra* within the Mahāyāna; in this sūtra it is said:
"How should the nature of discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) be known?
It should be known through the teaching that no categories of phenomena exist."
How should the dependent nature be understood?
It should be understood through its nature by means of such similes as an illusion, a mirage, the appearance of a dream, a reflection, light, an echo, the moon in water, and a magical transformation.
How should one understand true reality (*tathatā*)?
It should be understood through the teaching of the four kinds of pure phenomena (*caturvidha-viśuddhi-dharma*).

What are these four kinds of pure phenomena? First, this dharma is primordially pure by nature (*prakṛti-viśuddha*); that is to say, suchness (*tathatā*), emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), signlessness (*animitta*), truth (*satya*), and the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
Second is the purity of being stainless, which refers to this dharma’s emergence from all adventitious obscurations and defilements.
Third is the purity of attaining the path, which refers to all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) and the various perfections (*pāramitā*), and so forth.
The fourth is the purity of the sphere of birth for the four paths, which refers to the correct teaching of the Mahāyāna Dharma. Why is this?
Because this teaching is the cause of purity; it is not conceptual construction.
Because it flows from the pure dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), it is not dependent on others (*paratantra*).
By means of these four kinds of pure phenomena, all pure phenomena are fully subsumed.
Regarding this, a verse is spoken:
The appearance of illusions and the like reveals the dependent nature; the teaching that they are non-existent reveals the imagined nature.
If one speaks of the fourfold purity, this refers to the perfected nature.
Purity is due to its intrinsic nature, and it is the object-condition for the path of stainlessness.
All pure phenomena are subsumed within these four categories.
For what reason and by what cause is this the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*)?
It is as revealed by the analogies of illusions and so forth taught in the sūtras, intended to eliminate the false doubts of others regarding the dependent nature.
How do others give rise to false doubt regarding the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*)?
Various proponents harbor such false doubts concerning the dependent nature:
"If there are truly no entities, how can they constitute objects of perception?"
To resolve this doubt, the analogy of a magical illusion (*māyā*) is taught.
To resolve the further doubt as to how the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) could arise if there were no objective realm (*viṣaya*),
the analogy of a mirage (*marīci*) is taught.
If external objects do not truly exist, how can the experience of the pleasant and the unpleasant be established?
To resolve this doubt, the analogy of dream-phenomena is taught.
If no real dharmas exist, how can the retributive fruits of the pleasant and the unpleasant arise from the two types of karma—wholesome and unwholesome?
To resolve this doubt, the analogy of a shadow is taught. [One might ask:
"If no real entity exists, how can various cognitions arise?
To resolve this doubt, the analogy of light and shadow is taught.
If, in reality, there are no phenomena, how can various forms of verbal expression arise?
To resolve this doubt, the analogy of an echo is taught.
If, in reality, there are no phenomena, how can they become the objective domain of a concentrated mind that takes true dharmas as its conditions?
To resolve this doubt, the analogy of the moon in water is taught.
If phenomena were not real, how could the Bodhisattvas intentionally cultivate a mind free from inversion and take birth within the six realms of existence for the sake of benefiting others?
To resolve this doubt, the analogy of transformation is taught.
In the *Brahmaṇaparipṛcchā-sūtra*, it is said:
"World-Honored One!"
In what sense is it said that the Tathāgata perceives neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa?

Within the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva), based on the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) and the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva), saṃsāra serves as the basis for nirvāṇa; this is the meaning of their non-differentiation.

Why is this? This dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) constitutes saṃsāra through its aspect of conceptual construction (parikalpita), and constitutes nirvāṇa through its aspect of reality (pariniṣpanna).
In the Abhidharma Sūtras, the Blessed One taught that there are three kinds of dharmas:
First, the defiled portion; second, the purified portion; third, the portion that is both defiled and purified.
By what meaning are these three portions explained?

Within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) constitutes the defiled portion, the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) constitutes the purified portion, and the dependent nature itself constitutes the portion that is both defiled and purified.
Based on this meaning, three parts are taught.
Within this context, what serves as the analogy?
It is the analogy of gold hidden within the earth.
For example, within earth containing gold ore, three things are perceived:
first, the element of earth; second, gold; and third, soil.
Within this element of earth, the soil appears though it does not truly exist, while the gold truly exists though it does not appear.
If this earth were to be smelted with fire, the earth would no longer appear and the characteristics of gold would manifest of themselves.
When the earth-element appears in this ground, it does so through the manifestation of false appearances.
When gold becomes manifest, it is manifested through its true nature (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa*).
Therefore, the earth element has two aspects.

Likewise, when the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) has not yet been refined by the fire of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), this consciousness is manifested through its nature of false discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), and not through its true nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

When it is scorched and refined by the fire of non-conceptual wisdom, this consciousness manifests through the nature of perfected reality (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), and does not manifest through the nature of false discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

Therefore, the consciousness of the nature of false discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) possesses two aspects within its dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), just as the earth element exists within gold-bearing soil.

Furthermore, in some places the Blessed One has taught that all phenomena (*dharma*) are eternal; in other places, he has taught that all phenomena are impermanent; and in yet other places, he has taught that they are neither eternal nor impermanent.
In what sense is it said to be permanent?

This dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) is permanent from the perspective of its perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva), impermanent from the perspective of its imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva), and neither permanent nor impermanent from the perspective of both natures.

Just as it is said that permanence and impermanence are non-dual based on this meaning, so too are suffering and pleasure non-dual; good and evil are non-dual; emptiness and non-emptiness are non-dual; self and no-self are non-dual; tranquility and non-tranquility are non-dual; existence and non-existence are non-dual; arising and non-arising are non-dual; cessation and non-cessation are non-dual; primordial stillness and non-stillness are non-dual; primordial nirvana and non-nirvana are non-dual; and saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are non-dual.

Through such distinctions as these, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, employ intentional language (*saṃdhāyabhāṣita*) based on the meaning; by means of these three natures, one should correctly discern [the teachings] regarding permanence, impermanence, and so forth, as previously explained.
In this regard, a verse is spoken:
Just as phenomena do not exist in reality, yet appear in their various forms, Because of this, phenomena are both "dharma" and "adharma"; Therefore, it is said that they have no dual meaning.
Based on one aspect, it is said that there is existence or non-existence;
based on two aspects, it is said that there is neither existence nor non-existence.
Since things do not exist in the manner they appear, they are therefore said to be eternally non-existent.
Just as they appear to exist, they are therefore said not to be non-existent.
Because they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), because their intrinsic nature does not abide,
and because they do not exist in the manner they are grasped, the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) are established as being without intrinsic nature.
Established by way of non-existence, the former serves as the basis for the latter;
it is without arising or ceasing, primordially quiescent, and parinirvāṇa by its very nature.
Furthermore, there are four intentions and four reliances, according to which all the teachings of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, should be understood and resolved.
First, the intention of equality, as for example when it is said:
"In times past, my name was Vipaśyin; long ago I attained Buddhahood.
Second, the intention of a different time, as for example when it is said:
If a person recites and upholds the name of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna, they will certainly never again fall back from unsurpassed bodhi.
Furthermore, it is said that by merely making a vow for the Buddha-field of Sukhāvatī, one will attain rebirth there.
Third, regarding the meaning of the specific sense:
for example, it is said that one attains awakening to the meanings of the Mahāyāna Dharma through as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, such as those mentioned above.
Fourth, regarding the inclinations and desires of sentient beings: for example, the Tathāgata may first praise giving to one person, and later subsequently disparage it.
This is likewise true for giving, ethical discipline, and other practices as well.
These are called the four kinds of intention.

Regarding the four reliances: first is the reliance for entry, which is, for example, when the Buddha, the World-Honored One, within the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, teaches the conventional truth as comprised by the two general and specific characteristics of persons and phenomena.
Second is the basis of mutual dependence, which is like how within the characteristics of the teachings as they are expounded, the three natures must necessarily be present.
Third is the basis of counteractive measures, wherein the remedies for the eighty-four thousand afflictive tendencies of sentient beings are manifested.
Fourth, the reversal of reliance: herein, by means of words expressing a distinct meaning, an analogy for a distinct meaning is revealed.
As the verse says: *Asālisaramataye, vibhaye seṭṭhe sucitte.*
*Vinaya-saṃgraha*, *Saṃgha-kriyā*, *Lambanī-bodhi-vastu-mātṛkā*.

If one wishes to provide a detailed explanation of the Mahāyāna Dharma, it should be explained briefly by means of three characteristics: first, a detailed explanation of the essential nature and characteristics of dependent origination;

second, a detailed explanation of the true nature of all phenomena that have arisen based upon causes and conditions; and third, a detailed explanation of the establishment of the various meanings thus taught.
To explain extensively the essence and characteristics of dependent origination, as stated in the verse:

"The various dharmas produced by verbal perfuming arise from that; thus, the resultant consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) and the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) arise through mutual causality."

To explain in detail the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena (*dharma*) arisen from causes and conditions: "all phenomena" refers to those characterized by the arising consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), which has both the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Furthermore, all phenomena have the characteristic of dependence, the characteristic of conceptualization, and the characteristic of suchness; through these expressions, the essential characteristics of all phenomena within the three natures are revealed.
As it is said in verse:
"From the aspect of existence and the aspect of seeing, one should know the three characteristics of phenomena.
How can these characteristics of phenomena be explained?

The nature of conceptual differentiation (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) does not exist at all within the nature of dependence (*paratantra-svabhāva*), whereas the nature of reality (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) truly exists therein.
Because of this non-existence and existence of these two, the non-attainment and attainment, as well as the non-vision and vision of suchness, are spontaneously established simultaneously.

Within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), because the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is absent and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is present, if one perceives the former, one does not perceive the latter; and if one does not perceive the former, one perceives the latter.
As the verse says:
Within the dependent, the imagined Does not exist, while the perfected alone exists.
Therefore, non-attainment and attainment Are both equal therein.

Regarding the extensive explanation for establishing the various meanings stated: for example, the phrases stated at the outset are elucidated and analyzed by means of the subsequent phrases, either by way of reliance upon qualities (*guṇa*) or by way of reliance upon the meaning of the subject matter (*vastu*).
Regarding the basis of merit: it is the extensive exposition of the virtues of the Buddha, the World-Honored One— possessing the most purified wisdom,
acting without duality, taking the signless Dharma as his supreme reliance, and with mental activity abiding in the Buddha-abode—
until he attains the equal conduct and unimpeded conduct of all Buddhas, which is an indestructible, peerless, and irreversible Dharma that cannot be altered.
Diverse realms are inconceivable; the dharmas established therein reach equality throughout the three periods of time.
He manifests his body in all worlds, possesses unimpeded wisdom regarding all dharmas, and his every action accords with wisdom.
He has no doubt regarding the knowledge of dharmas, possesses an indivisible body, and is [the refuge] for all bodhisattvas.
Having received wisdom, they reach the perfection of dwelling in the non-dual Buddha-state;

they reach the non-differentiated Tathāgata’s liberative knowledge, having ultimately attained the boundless Buddha-ground. With the equal dharma-realm as supreme, the realm of empty space serves as its ultimate limit.
O Viśuddhamati, this first phrase should be understood as being analyzed and explained sequentially by means of the remaining phrases.

If the meaning of the Dharma is correctly taught in this way so that it becomes most pure wisdom, then the wisdom of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, is pure regarding all phenomena and there is nothing they do not discern; this fundamental meaning should be known as being subsumed within twenty-one Buddha-qualities.

The merit of engaging in unimpeded activity regarding all that is to be known; the merit of causing entry into the most pure *tathatā*, which is characterized by the non-duality of existence and non-existence;
the merit of the Buddha’s dwelling, which does not abandon the activities of a Tathāgata without effort;
and the merit of the non-distinction between the basis of the *dharmakāya* and its intentional activities—[these are] the cultivation of all [merits].
The merit of counteracting hindrances; the merit of subduing all non-Buddhists;
the merit of being born into the world yet remaining unstained by worldly dharmas; the merit of establishing the True Dharma;
the merit of fourfold skillfulness in answering the questions of others; and the merit of manifesting transformation bodies throughout all worlds.
The merit of being able to resolve the doubts of others; the merit of being able to cause others to enter [the path] through various practices;
the merit of generating knowledge regarding phenomena in future lives; the merit of manifesting according to the inclinations of sentient beings;
the merit of being able to perform immeasurable deeds of correct teaching based upon sentient beings; and the perfection of the equal *dharmakāya*.
Regarding merit: it is the merit of manifesting pure buddha-fields in accordance with the inclinations of sentient beings;

it is the merit of the three bodies of the Buddha being inseparable and non-distinct in their location; and it is the merit of being able to produce the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings until the very end of saṃsāra, by virtue of its inexhaustible merit.
Regarding the basis for the meaning of the causal factors, as the Sūtra says:
"If a bodhisattva is endowed with thirty-two qualities, he is called a bodhisattva.

He is endowed with the intention to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings and the intention to lead them into the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*). [He reflects: "In what state should I now be endowed with such wisdom?"

Abandoning pride, one should maintain a firm and virtuous intention; not feigning compassion, one should not crave gratitude in return; maintaining an even mind toward both friends and enemies, one should forever act as a true friend.
Even unto the nirvana without remainder, he speaks with measured words and a smile, being the first to address others; his compassion for all sentient beings is without distinction;
in all that he does, he possesses no heart of retreat or weakness and no heart of weariness; he is never satiated in hearing the Dharma;
he is able to reveal his own transgressions, yet he does not find fault in or condemn the transgressions committed by others.
Constantly maintaining the bodhicitta throughout all modes of conduct; practicing generosity without seeking karmic rewards;
upholding the precepts without attachment to any fears or the sensations arising on the path;
practicing patience toward all sentient beings without obstruction; exerting diligence to attract and gather all wholesome dharmas; and cultivating samādhi.
He transcends the formless absorptions (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) and possesses wisdom conjoined with skillful means (*upāya*).
He employs skillful means conjoined with the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), maintaining no dualism toward friends whether they uphold or violate the precepts.

He serves spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), listens to the Dharma with a respectful mind, and dwells joyfully in forest hermitages (*araṇya*) with a respectful mind; he does not give rise to worldly aspirations.
With a mind of peace and happiness, they do not give rise to a mind of delight in the inferior vehicles;
they contemplate the true merits within the Mahāyāna teachings, distance themselves from evil friends, and respectfully serve virtuous friends.
They constantly cultivate the four kinds of Brahma-vihāras, purify the immeasurable minds, constantly sport in the five supernormal powers, and always act in reliance upon wisdom.
Toward sentient beings who abide in correct practice or do not abide in correct practice, he maintains no mind of abandonment and draws in the great assembly.
His speech is consistently definitive.
He honors the reality of things and practices the bodhisattva-mind that first honors such conduct.
One who is endowed with such qualities as these is called a bodhisattva.
By means of this passage, it should be understood that the first phrase previously mentioned is being explained.
The "first phrase" refers to the intention for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings.
Regarding these phrases expressing the intention for benefit and happiness, it should be understood that there is a distinct exposition of the activities manifested by sixteen phrases.
The sixteen activities are:
first, the activity of continuous transmission (*saṃtati-karma*).
2. Unmistaken action;
3. Action performed independently of others;
4. Indestructible action.

Regarding the five types of action free from seeking desire, one should know that there are three explanatory points: not coveting a reward for one's kindness; not giving rise to feelings of attachment or aversion toward sentient beings whether they have been kind or unkind; and practicing accordingly throughout successive lives and in all circumstances.
Regarding the activity of corresponding discourse, it should be understood that there are two phrases of explanation:
the activity of equality toward sentient beings who possess suffering, pleasure, or neither;
and the activity of being without inferiority.
The karma that prevents regression;
the karma that encompasses skillful means;
and the karma that brings about aversion toward what is to be countered.
It should be understood that there are two phrases of explanation:

the activity of uninterrupted reflection and the activity of advancing toward superior states. It should be understood that there are seven phrases of explanation: the correct cultivation of the application of the six pāramitās and the respectful practice of the four means of attraction (saṃgrahavastu).
Regarding the accomplishment of the activity of skillful means, one should understand that there are six points of explanation: serving spiritual friends;
hearing the true Dharma;
and dwelling in forest hermitages.
One should remain far removed from wrong thoughts and reflections.
Regarding the virtues of right reflection (*samyak-saṃkalpa*), there are two phrases;

regarding the manifestation of the virtues of associating with a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), there are two phrases; and regarding the manifestation of the accomplishment of activity, there are three phrases of explanation to be understood: the cultivation of the immeasurable minds, purification, and the attainment of majestic power (*prabhāva*).

Regarding the establishment of others through the realization of merit, there are four points of explanation to be understood: gathering the great assembly, establishing the training rules of the true teaching without doubt, the two types of gathering—through Dharma and material wealth—and possessing a mind free from defilement.
One should understand that such phrases explain the textual passages stated at the beginning.
Herein, a verse says:
"Taking up the phrases as previously explained, according to the distinctions of the qualities of the phrases,"
Taking up the phrases as previously explained, [the distinctions] arise from the distinction of meaning and the distinction of phrases.

3. It should be known that this is included in the Chapter on the Superior Characteristics of Entry. Thus has been explained the superior characteristic of what is to be known (*jñeya-lakṣaṇa*). *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, Chapter Three: "It Should Be Known That the Superior Characteristics of Entry. Thus, the superior characteristic of what is to be known has already been explained.
How should one understand the superior characteristics of the object to be known?
It is the basis perfumed by extensive learning; it is not subsumed within the *ālaya-vijñāna*, yet it functions as a seed in the same manner as the *ālaya-vijñāna*.

What kind of person can enter into the characteristic of what is to be known— the mental verbal discrimination accompanied by an appearance that resembles the dharma and its meaning, which is produced by the appearance of the object as it is grasped,
and which is subsumed under right reflection?

Having established a continuity of the Mahāyāna through the perfuming of extensive learning, they have attained the service of immeasurable supramundane Buddhas; having entered the stage of definitive faith and joy, their roots of goodness have been well-matured, cultivated, and increased, whereby they have successfully acquired the two kinds of provisions: merit and wisdom.
In what state do the bodhisattvas enter the contemplation of representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*)?

They enter it through the mental verbalization (*manojalpa*) that manifests as the appearance of objects resembling phenomena (*dharma-artha*), which arises from the characteristics of the Mahāyāna teachings. This occurs at the stage of practice through aspiration (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), because they follow what they have heard with faith and delight; at the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), because they penetrate reality according to principle; at the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), because they are able to counteract all obstacles; and within the ultimate path (*niṣṭhā-mārga*), because they have emerged from the stains of obstacles and are most pure.

All phenomena are in reality nothing but consciousness, because one believes and delights in them according to what has been heard, because one penetrates them through correct reasoning, because they can counteract all obstacles, and because they emerge from the defilements of obstacles to become supremely pure.
How does one enter?
By being sustained by the power of the roots of goodness; by exercising the three modes of mental refinement;
and by eliminating the obstructions of the four bases.
Taking the meaning of the Dharma as one’s object, one practices śamatha and vipaśyanā through uninterrupted cultivation and reverent cultivation, being free from negligence.

Because the worlds of the ten directions are immeasurable, there are incalculable numbers of sentient beings in the human realm who, moment by moment, realize unsurpassed enlightenment; this is called the first exercise of the mind.
By means of this correct intention, the perfections such as generosity will certainly grow and flourish; thus my faith and delight have already attained firm stability.
By means of this correct intention, it will not be difficult for me to practice the perfections such as generosity until they reach fulfillment; this is called the second refinement of the mind.
If a person is endowed with various wholesome dharmas, then at the time of death, all desirable wealth and happiness will arise spontaneously throughout every future birth.

Since it follows that such a person would attain obstructed wholesome states, how much more so should I—possessing both perfect wholesome states and unobstructed wholesome states—not attain all manner of desirable wealth and happiness according to my wishes?
This is called the third refinement of the mind.
Regarding this, a verse is spoken:
"Sentient beings within the human realm Realize bodhi in every thought-moment."
Because the locations and the number [of recipients] are immeasurable, there is no inferiority of mind.
Those with virtuous minds have faith and joy, and are able to give rise to the perfections such as giving;
superior persons who attain this intention are thus able to cultivate giving and the other perfections.
If a virtuous person at the time of death attains supreme wealth and happiness, and their state of cessation is perfectly pure and wholesome—how could this principle not exist?

It is because they have eliminated the obstructions of the four bases; because they have abandoned the mental orientations of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; because false mental orientation has ceased and they have generated faith and a mind of definitive resolve toward the Mahāyāna; and because all perverse intentions and doubts have been extinguished.
Because one abandons the false attachments to "self" and "what belongs to self" regarding all phenomena heard and contemplated, one thereby eliminates the attachment to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*).

By establishing and dwelling in the presence of the mental attention (*manasikāra*) toward all signs (*nimitta*) without making any conceptual distinctions, one is thus able to eliminate conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
Regarding this, a verse is spoken:
"Manifestly abiding and established, all mental engagement with signs—
the wise do not discriminate these, and thus attain unsurpassed awakening."
Taking the phenomena (*dharma*) and their meanings (*artha*) as objects, by what cause and by what means does one enter [into them]?

It is because of the conceptualization of mental discourse (*manojalpa-vikalpa*)—which is comprised of correct reflection (*yoniśo-manasikāra*) of the type resulting from the cultivation of hearing—that there appears the semblance of phenomena and their meanings. This occurs through the four kinds of thorough investigation (*paryeṣaṇā*), namely:

the investigation of names (*nāma*), the investigation of objects (*artha*), the investigation of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and the investigation of specific differences (*viśeṣa*). These are investigations into conventional designations (*prajñapti*).
By means of four kinds of knowledge as it truly is—namely, the knowledge of names, meanings, intrinsic natures, and distinctions—as these four are not to be found.
If a bodhisattva has already entered into and understood such meanings, they then cultivate preparatory practices for the sake of entering the contemplation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).

Within this contemplation, the conceptualization of mental discourse manifests as if it were syllables, words, and meanings; herein, one attains such penetration that the characteristic of syllables and words is understood to be merely conceptualization of mental discourse.
This meaning relies upon conventional designations as mere mental verbalization; one should likewise penetrate this.
That the self-nature and specific differences of names and meanings are merely designated as valid measures should likewise be penetrated.
Next, within this stage, one realizes that there is only the conceptualization of mental discourse;

thus, the practitioner does not perceive names or objects, nor does he perceive the conventional designations of intrinsic nature or specific difference, because in the true nature of reality, neither intrinsic nature nor specific difference can exist.

By means of the four kinds of thorough investigation and the four kinds of knowledge as it truly is, one enters the contemplation of representation-only (*vijñaptimātratā*) regarding the mental-linguistic conceptualization that manifests as names and objects.
In the contemplation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*),

into what phenomena does one enter, and by what means is entry attained? One enters into mere-cognition (*vijñaptimātra*) alone, because the two factors of the grasped-image (*nimitta*) and the grasping-seeing (*darśana*), along with their various characteristics— the names, objects, intrinsic natures, distinctions, and the meanings of the conventional designations of intrinsic nature and distinction— these six aspects are devoid of objective reality.
Because the grasper and the grasped do not exist as substantial entities, they manifest simultaneously, appearing as various characteristics and arising.
This is like a vine appearing as a snake in the dark; just as the snake within the vine is empty and does not truly exist.

If a person has already discerned the meaning of this vine, the previous deluded cognition of a snake—which arose without an objective referent—immediately ceases, and only the cognition of the vine remains.
Through subtle analysis, this cognition of the vine is further deconstructed, revealing that even "space" lacks any real objective referent.
Why is this? Because it is merely the characteristics of form, odor, taste, and touch.
If the mind takes these objects as its conditions, then even the cognition of the vine should be extinguished.

If, having seen it thus, [the mind] subdues and extinguishes [the grasping], the six aspects manifest as if they were names and objects; yet the mental verbalization (*manojalpa*) and the cognition of objects do not arise, just like the cognition of a snake [when the rope is known].

Within the context of subduing and extinguishing the meaning of the six characteristics, this wisdom of representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*) should likewise be subdued and extinguished, just as the cognition of a vine [is sublated by the cognition of its constituent parts], because it relies upon the wisdom of suchness (*tathatā*).

In this way, by entering into the aspect of the mental verbalization that appears as if it were an external object, the bodhisattva enters into the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); by entering into the meaning of "consciousness-only" (*vijñapti-mātra*), he enters into the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). But how does he enter into the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*)?

When the perception of representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*) has been relinquished, at that time, the mental verbalization (*manojalpa-vikalpa*)—which is of the nature of the habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*) from previously heard teachings—the Bodhisattva has already discerned and suppressed the perception of objects (*artha-saṃjñā*). Because there are no longer any conditions for its arising, that which appears as all objective referents cannot arise; consequently, the mental verbalization appearing as representation-only also cannot arise.

For this reason, the bodhisattva dwells solely within the non-conceptualization of all objects and names; through non-conceptual wisdom, they attain realization and abide in the *dharmadhātu* of *tathatā*.

At that time, the Bodhisattva gives rise to non-conceptual wisdom in which the subject and object are perfectly equal; by virtue of this principle, the Bodhisattva enters into true reality (*tathatā*).
In this regard, a verse is spoken:
The person and the phenomena, their meaning, Their nature, the brief and the extensive names,
Impurity, purity, and the ultimate— These ten names are the differentiated objects.
In this way, because the bodhisattva enters the contemplation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), they attain entry into the superior characteristics of what is to be known (*jñeyalakṣaṇa*).

By entering these characteristics, they attain entry into the first stage, the Joyful (*pramuditā-bhūmi*); they thoroughly penetrate the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); they are born into the family of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions; they attain equality of mind with all sentient beings; they attain equality of mind with all bodhisattvas; and they attain equality of mind with all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas. This contemplation is called the bodhisattva’s path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

Furthermore, for what reason does the Bodhisattva enter the contemplation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*)? It is because they possess the supramundane wisdom of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* which takes the extremely pervasive dharma as its object; because they possess the wisdom that takes the various marks of consciousness subsequently attained after non-conceptual wisdom as its characteristic; in order to eliminate all seeds of dharmas possessing causes within the common fundamental *ālayavijñāna*; in order to cultivate and grow the seeds of those dharmas capable of touching the *dharmakāya*; in order to achieve the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*); in order to attain all the true dharmas of the Tathāgatas; and in order to attain the wisdom of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*). For these reasons, one enters the contemplation of consciousness-only.

Regarding the subsequently attained wisdom following non-conceptual wisdom: with respect to the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) and all the consciousnesses produced from it—both the cognitions and their objective aspects—one observes them through analogies such as magical illusions and the like; thus, its intrinsic nature is free from inversion.

For this reason, the bodhisattva is like a magician who thoroughly understands all illusory phenomena without error; when correctly explaining all marks, causes, conditions, and effects, he is always free from bias or inversion.
At this time, while entering the stage of the contemplation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), there are four kinds of samādhi.
These are the bases for the four kinds of roots of goodness conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
How should a bodhisattva perceive them?

Through four kinds of thorough investigation, one attains the samādhi of the light of receptivity toward the contemplation of the non-existence of objects at the lower stage; this is the basis for the roots of goodness of the "heat" stage within the factors conducive to penetration.

The samādhi of the increase of light (*ālokavṛddhi*) within the supreme stage of receptivity toward the non-existence of objects (*anupalambha-kṣānti*) is the basis for the roots of virtue conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) at the stage of the summit (*mūrdhan*).

Because the bodhisattva has entered the contemplation of representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*) and discerned the non-existence of objects through the four kinds of knowledge of reality as it is (*yathābhūtaparijñāna*), they correctly enter the samādhi of partial penetration into true reality (*tattvārtha-ekadeśapraveśa*). This is the basis for the receptivity toward the non-conceptualized truth (*apratiṣṭhita-satya-kṣānti*).

At the final moment of this samādhi, one completely subdues the perception of representation-only (vijñaptimātra); it is then renamed "uninterrupted samādhi" (ānantarya-samādhi), which should be understood as the basis for the highest mundane dharma (laukikāgra-dharma).
The four kinds of samādhi are the preliminary expedients for a bodhisattva’s entry into the contemplation of the non-established truths.
Once a bodhisattva has thus entered the first stage (bhūmi) and attained the path of seeing (darśanamārga), they attain penetration and entry into consciousness-only (vijñaptimātra).
How does a bodhisattva cultivate contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) to enter the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)?

As the Buddha has extensively explained, the established characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) within the ten bodhisattva stages (*daśabhūmi*) become manifest through the inclusion of all twelve divisions of the Mahāyāna sūtras spoken by the Tathāgatas.

Based on the mastery of the two types of objects—general and specific—as previously explained; based on the arising of supramundane non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) and the wisdom of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) subsequently attained after that non-conceptual wisdom, which take the most universal objects as their conditions; based on the repeated cultivation throughout immeasurable, innumerable hundreds of thousands of millions of great eons (*kalpa*); and based on the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) attained both in the past and the present—one further cultivates preparatory application (*prayoga*) in order to attain the three bodies of a Buddha.
This is the path of seeing of the śrāvaka and this is the path of seeing of the bodhisattva; what is the distinction between these two paths of seeing?
It should be understood that there are eleven kinds of distinctions between the paths of seeing of the śrāvakas and the bodhisattvas.
What are these eleven?
First, by way of the distinction of the object: that is, taking the Mahāyāna Dharma as its object.
Second, by way of the distinction of the basis: that is, relying upon the accumulation of great merit and wisdom as its basis.
Third, by way of the distinction of thorough penetration, which refers to thoroughly penetrating the two kinds of selflessness—of persons and of phenomena.
Fourth, by way of the distinction of nirvāṇa, which refers to taking non-abiding nirvāṇa as one’s dwelling place.
Fifth, by way of the distinction of stages (*bhūmi*), it means that one takes the ten stages as the means of transcendence.
Sixth and seventh, by way of the distinction of purification, it means that the purification consists of eliminating the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of afflictions and purifying the buddha-field.

Eighth, it is due to the distinction of attaining a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings; that is, for the sake of maturing sentient beings, one does not abandon the application of effort, merit, and roots of goodness.
Ninth, by way of the distinction of birth: that is, being born into the family of the Tathāgatas for the sake of birth.
Tenth, by way of the distinction of manifestation: that is, being constantly able to manifest within the great assemblies of the Buddha's sons in order to uphold the True Dharma.
Eleventh, by way of the distinction of results: this refers to the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the unique qualities of a Tathāgata, and the arising of immeasurable virtues as the result.
Regarding this, two verses are spoken:
Name and meaning are mutually adventitious; The Bodhisattva should investigate them.
One should contemplate that both are merely mental constructs, as well as their conventional designations.
From this, true wisdom arises; by abandoning the three types of conceptualization regarding objects, and seeing that they do not exist, one enters the three natures of non-existence.
Furthermore, there are two verses from the orthodox teaching as stated in the *Vibhanga-viniścaya-śāstra*:
"When a bodhisattva abides in the state of tranquility, He contemplates that the mind is nothing but a reflection;
Having abandoned the appearances of external objects, He contemplates only his own mental constructs through meditative concentration."
"The Bodhisattva abiding within enters into the non-existence of the grasped;
next, he contemplates the emptiness of the grasper; finally, he touches the non-apprehension of both.
Furthermore, there are five verses from the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* spoken to reveal this path.
“Bodhisattvas cultivate merit and wisdom; these two provisions are immeasurable in their extent.
Because their minds are resolved through reflection on the Dharma, they are able to comprehend the categories of meaning and discern their causes.”
Knowing that objects and their categories are merely conceptual constructions, one abides within consciousness-only which appears as objects;
thus, the practitioner realizes the dharmadhātu, able to transcend both duality and non-duality.
If one realizes that nothing exists apart from the mind, thereby seeing that the mind itself does not exist;
when the wise perceive that these two do not exist, they dwell in the non-dual true dharmadhātu.
By means of non-conceptual wisdom, the person of realization constantly practices equanimity throughout all things;
the dense accumulation of defilements and faults is dispelled and extinguished, just as medicine can eliminate poison.
The Buddha has well established the True Dharma; With a mind settled, it is rooted in the Dharmadhātu.
Knowing that recollection is merely conceptual construction, The wise one reaches the shore of merit.

4. Chapter on Entering the Superior Characteristics of Cause and Result (*Praveśa-hetu-phala-viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*). Thus has been explained the entry into the superior characteristics of that which is to be known (*jñeya*). *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, Chapter Four: Entering the Superior Characteristics of Cause and Result.
How should one understand the superior characteristics of entering into cause and effect?
They are known by means of the six pāramitās, namely: dāna-pāramitā, śīla-pāramitā, kṣānti-pāramitā, vīrya-pāramitā, dhyāna-pāramitā, and prajñā-pāramitā.
How does one enter *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) by means of the six *pāramitās*, and how do the six *pāramitās* become the fruit of entering *vijñapti-mātra*?

Within this True Dharma, there are bodhisattvas who possess no attachment to wealth and pleasure in their minds, no mind of transgression regarding the precepts, no mind of despair regarding suffering, and no mind of indolence in the cultivation of virtue. Because they do not dwell in or cling to these causes of distraction, they constantly practice single-mindedness and discern all phenomena according to reality, thereby attaining entry into the contemplation of *vijñapti-mātra*.

By relying on the six pāramitās, the bodhisattva has already entered the stage of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra-bhūmi*), and subsequently attains the six pāramitās embraced by the mental state of pure faith and aspiration (*śraddhā-prasāda-manasikāra*).

Therefore, even during this intermediate stage, although one may be devoid of the application and effort of the six pāramitās, by virtue of faith and delight in the correct teaching, cherishing it, rejoicing in it, aspiring for its attainment, and reflecting upon it, and because one practices constantly without rest, one brings the cultivation of the six pāramitās to ultimate perfection.
A verse is spoken herein:
By cultivating the perfectly pure dharmas, One is able to attain sharp and swift patience;
Regarding their own vehicle, the Bodhisattvas Proclaim what is profound and vast.
Because one realizes that [all things] are mere conceptual construction, and because one attains non-attached wisdom, this joyful faith is pure;
it is called the stage of the pure mental ground (*viśuddhamanobhūmi*).
The Bodhisattva, abiding in the flow of the Dharma, perceives all Buddhas before and after.
Knowing that awakening is near because it is easily attained without difficulty, one may ask:
why are there exactly six perfections (*pāramitā*)? They are established in order to counteract the obstacles of the six types of afflictions;

to serve as the basis for the arising of all Buddha-dharmas; to serve as the support for maturing all sentient beings in accordance with their needs; and to counteract the causes for failing to initiate the practice. Thus, the two perfections of giving (*dāna*) and ethical discipline (*śīla*) are established.
The causes for not generating the mind of practice are attachment to wealth and family.
If one has already generated the mind for practice, the two pāramitās of patience and diligence are established as antidotes to the causes that lead to the weakening of that mind.

The causes for the weakening of the mind refer to the opposition of sentient beings within saṃsāra, the protracted nature of tasks, and the exhaustion resulting from the application of effort toward the cultivation of wholesome dharmas.

Since the practice has already been initiated and the mind is not yet weakened, the two pāramitās of concentration and wisdom are established as remedies against the causes that lead to the ruin and loss of the mind.
The causes for the ruin and loss of the mind are distraction and false wisdom.
Therefore, in order to counteract these six kinds of afflictive obstacles, the perfections (pāramitās) are established as being six in number.

Regarding the phrase "because it is the basis for the arising of all Buddha-dharmas": the first four pāramitās are the causes of non-distraction, while the subsequent one pāramitā is the essence of non-distraction.
By relying on this non-distraction, one is able to realize the true nature of all phenomena as it is, and thus all the sublime teachings of the Tathāgatas are brought forth.

Therefore, because they serve as the basis for the arising of all Buddha-dharmas, the pāramitās are established as being six in number. Regarding their function as the support for maturing all sentient beings in accordance with their needs:

through the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), one benefits sentient beings; through the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), one does not harm or afflict them; through the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), one is able to endure their insults and slanders without giving rise to a mind of retribution; and through the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*), one generates roots of goodness in them and extinguishes their roots of evil. By means of these beneficial causes, all sentient beings become disciplined. Subsequently, for those whose minds have not yet attained tranquility, one establishes the perfections of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) in order to bring about that tranquility; and for those who have already attained tranquility, one establishes them in order to bring about liberation. Thus, the two perfections of concentration and wisdom are established.

By means of these six perfections, bodhisattvas skillfully instruct sentient beings and thereby bring them to maturity; for this reason, they serve as the basis for conforming to the maturation of all sentient beings, and thus the perfections are established as being six in number.
Based on this meaning, one should understand that the establishment of the perfections (pāramitās) consists of six in number.
How are the characteristics of these six perfections to be seen?
There are six common characteristics of the six supreme perfections:
First, by way of the incomparable basis, meaning it arises based on the unsurpassed bodhicitta.
Second, by way of the incomparable categories, meaning that each *pāramitā* is briefly said to have three grades, all of which the bodhisattva fully practices.

Third, by way of the peerlessness of their activities: this refers to the activities for the peace, happiness, and benefit of all sentient beings; for all the perfections practiced by Bodhisattvas are undertaken solely to accomplish these two purposes.
Fourth, they are peerless by way of skillful means (*upāya*), meaning that the perfections practiced by Bodhisattvas are all subsumed within non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).

Fifth, they are peerless by way of dedication (*pariṇāmana*), meaning that the perfections practiced by Bodhisattvas are dedicated toward unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-bodhi*) and thus inevitably lead toward the fruit of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).

Sixth, by way of incomparable purity: this refers to the eternal extinction of the two obstacles—those of afflictions and of knowledge—without remainder; for the various perfections practiced by Bodhisattvas eliminate these two obstacles stage by stage until they are entirely exhausted.
Is giving itself the pāramitā, and the pāramitā itself giving? There is that which is giving but not a pāramitā;
there is that which is a pāramitā but not giving; there is that which is both giving and a pāramitā; and there is that which is neither giving nor a pāramitā.
Just as there are four permutations regarding giving, one should know that the other perfections likewise possess four permutations.
Why are the six pāramitās taught in this specific order?
Because each preceding pāramitā is conducive to the successive arising of each subsequent pāramitā.
Furthermore, since each preceding perfection is purified by each subsequent perfection,
on what basis are the names of the six perfections established?
How is this meaning to be understood?

Because it is the most supreme and peerless among all the roots of goodness—such as generosity—of all worldly beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas, and because it is able to reach the further shore, it is therefore collectively termed a *pāramitā*.
Because it can destroy stinginess, jealousy, and the suffering of poverty and low status, it is called *da*.
Furthermore, because it enables one to become a great lord of wealth and to draw forth the provisions of merit, it is called *na*.
Because it can pacify wrong conduct and evil destinies, it is called *śī* (尸).
Furthermore, because it can cause one to attain good destinies and *samādhi*, it is termed *la* (羅).
Because it can eliminate hatred and resentment, it is called *kṣā* (羼).
Furthermore, because it can produce peaceful matters for oneself and others, it is called *ti*.
Because it can eliminate laziness and all unwholesome dharmas, it is named *vīri*.
Moreover, because it practices non-negligence and causes immeasurable wholesome dharmas to grow, it is called *ya*.
Because it can extinguish and eliminate distraction, it is called *kha*;
because it can lead the mind to abide within its internal object, it is called *na*;
and because it can extinguish all modes of viewing (*dṛṣṭi*) and eliminate false wisdom, it is called *prā*.
Because it can take the true nature as its object and knows all phenomena according to their respective categories, it is called "if" (jue).
How should one understand the cultivation of the various pāramitās?
Briefly stated, one should know that there are five kinds of cultivation:

First, the cultivation of the methods of preparatory application; second, the cultivation of faith and aspiration; third, the cultivation of reflection; fourth, the cultivation of superior wisdom regarding skillful means; and fifth, the cultivation of activities for the benefit of others.
Among these, it should be understood that the first four types of cultivation are as previously explained.

Regarding the cultivation for the sake of benefiting others: through the effortless application of the Buddhas, they do not abandon the activities of a Tathāgata while practicing the pāramitās, and they continue to cultivate the pāramitās even upon reaching the stage of perfection.

Furthermore, regarding the cultivation through reflection: the six intentions that encompass the practice cultivated through the reflection on cherishing, sympathetic joy, and the aspiration for attainment are: first, the expansive intention; second, the long-term intention; third, the joyful intention; fourth, the intentional of gratitude and virtue; fifth, the resolute intention; and sixth, the virtuous intention.

Regarding the vast intention: suppose a bodhisattva were able to attain unsurpassed enlightenment after a certain number of asaṃkhyeya kalpas; taking such a duration as a single kṣaṇa, and within each such kṣaṇa constantly sacrificing their own body and life, and offering as a gift and support to the Tathāgata the seven treasures filling worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—from the first generation of the mind of enlightenment until entering and abiding in the ultimate, cool state of Bodhi—even then, this bodhisattva’s intention for giving would still not be satisfied.

For such a long time, amidst the blazing fires that fill the trichiliocosm moment by moment, the Bodhisattva performs the four postures of walking, standing, sitting, and lying down; though devoid of all the necessities for sustaining life, the Bodhisattva constantly practices with a mind of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom ever present before them.
Even until they enter and abide in ultimate, cool enlightenment, the Bodhisattva’s resolve regarding the precepts, patience, and so forth remains unsatisfied.
This mind of insatiability is called the Bodhisattva’s vast intention.

If a bodhisattva, from the first generation of the mind of enlightenment until the attainment of Buddhahood, does not abandon the mind of insatiable diligence, this is called the bodhisattva’s long-term intention (*dīrghakālika-āśaya*).

If a bodhisattva, through the beneficial deeds for others performed by means of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), constantly gives rise to incomparable joy—such that the joy felt when sentient beings obtain benefit cannot compare to it—this is called the bodhisattva’s joyful intention (*pramuditā-āśaya*).

If a bodhisattva, having benefited sentient beings by practicing the six pāramitās, perceives that sentient beings possess great kindness and virtue toward him, while not perceiving himself as possessing kindness toward them, this is called the bodhisattva’s mind of gratitude and virtue.

If a bodhisattva bestows upon all sentient beings the roots of goodness and merit born from the six pāramitās, dedicating them with a mind free from attachment so that they may obtain desirable and weighty fruits of retribution, this is called the great resolve of a bodhisattva.

If a bodhisattva causes all sentient beings to equally attain the merit and roots of goodness from the six pāramitās they practice, dedicating them toward unexcelled bodhi, this is called the bodhisattva’s wholesome intention.

By means of this cultivation of loving and respectful reflection encompassed by these six intentions, if a bodhisattva rejoices in the roots of virtue and merit arising from the application of the six intentions cultivated by immeasurable bodhisattvas, this is called the bodhisattva’s reflection of rejoicing encompassed by the six intentions.

If a bodhisattva vows that all sentient beings shall practice the six pāramitās as subsumed by the six intentions, and vows for themselves to practice the six pāramitās as subsumed by the six intentions, cultivating these preparatory applications until the attainment of buddhahood, this is called the bodhisattva’s contemplation on the vow subsumed by the six intentions.

If a person hears of this contemplative cultivation of a bodhisattva as encompassed by the six intentions and gives rise to even a single thought of faith, that person shall obtain an immeasurable and boundless accumulation of merit, and all their evil karmic obstructions will be destroyed and extinguished without remainder.
If even those who merely hear [of these perfections] obtain immeasurable and boundless merit, how much more so for Bodhisattvas who are able to practice them fully.
How should one understand the distinctions among the various pāramitās?
Their distinctions are known through the fact that each consists of three grades.
The three grades of giving are: first, the gift of Dharma; second, the gift of material wealth; and third, the gift of fearlessness.
The three grades of ethical discipline are: first, the discipline of restraint; second, the discipline of gathering virtuous dharmas; and third, the discipline of benefiting sentient beings.
The three grades of patience are: first, patience toward insults and humiliation from others; second, patience in enduring suffering; and third, patience through the observation of dharmas.
The three grades of diligence are: first, the diligence of courageous exertion; second, the diligence of applied practice; and third, the diligence that is indefatigable, unbreakable, and insatiable.
The three categories of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) are: first, the concentration for dwelling in peace and happiness; second, the concentration that induces supernormal powers (*abhijñā*);

and third, the concentration that accords with benefiting others. The three categories of wisdom (*prajñā*) are: first, non-conceptual preparatory wisdom; second, non-conceptual wisdom; and third, non-conceptual subsequently attained wisdom.
How should one understand the meaning of the inclusion of all perfections?

All wholesome dharmas are subsumed within the six perfections because they constitute their very nature, because they are the outflowing fruits of those six perfections, and because they are accomplished in accordance with them.
How should one understand the inclusion of the factors to be countered by the various pāramitās?
Because all afflictions constitute their nature, because they are the cause for their arising, and because they are the outflowing results thereof.
How should one understand the merits of the *pāramitās*?

If a bodhisattva revolves within birth and death, they are encompassed by the state of great wealth and sovereignty, encompassed by noble birth, encompassed by a great retinue and assembly, encompassed by the accomplishment of great means of livelihood and activities, encompassed by freedom from illness and affliction, fewness of desires, and so forth, and encompassed by intelligence regarding all fields of arts and sciences; for they bring about the welfare of sentient beings through rightful deeds with such effortless and unerring abundance and prosperity.
Because the merit of a bodhisattva’s cultivation of the six perfections remains constant and unchanging from its inception until the entry into the ultimate, cool state of bodhi.
How should one understand that the various pāramitās mutually manifest one another?

The World-Honored One sometimes explains the various pāramitās by the name of "giving," or by the name of "precept," or by the name of "patience," or by the name of "diligence," or by the name of "concentration," or by the name of "wisdom."
With what intention did the Tathāgata speak thus?
It is because within the skillful means of practicing one pāramitā, all other pāramitās are gathered together and provide assistance toward its fulfillment.
This is precisely the intended meaning of the Tathāgata’s teaching.
Regarding this, there is a summary verse (*udāna*) that says:
"Stages, numbers, characteristics, and sequence; Names, cultivation, distinctions, and inclusion."
The remedies and the virtues mutually elucidate the meaning of the perfections.
